chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: Ancient Greek philosophy was divided into three sciences: physics, ethics, and logic. This division suits the nature of the subject perfectly. The only improvement we can make is to add the principle on which the division rests, so that we can confirm its completeness and identify its necessary subdivisions correctly.

All rational knowledge is either material or formal. Formal knowledge deals only with the form of understanding and reason itself, with the universal laws of thought, regardless of what those thoughts are about. Material knowledge deals with specific objects and the laws that govern them. Formal philosophy is called logic. Material philosophy, which concerns definite objects and the laws to which they are subject, splits in two: the laws are either laws of nature or laws of freedom. The science of the first is physics, the science of the second is ethics. They are also called natural philosophy and moral philosophy.

Logic cannot have any empirical part — that is, no part where the universal and necessary laws of thought would rest on grounds drawn from experience. Otherwise it would not be logic at all, but only a fallible record of how people happen to think. A canon for understanding and reason, valid for all thought and demonstrable, must be entirely a priori. Natural and moral philosophy, on the other hand, can each have an empirical part. Physics has to determine the laws of nature as an object of experience; ethics has to determine the laws of the human will as it is affected by nature. The laws of physics describe how everything actually happens; the laws of ethics describe how everything ought to happen. Ethics must also take account of the conditions under which what ought to happen often does not.

We may call all philosophy empirical so far as it rests on grounds of experience. The philosophy that derives its doctrines from a priori principles alone we may call pure philosophy. When pure philosophy is merely formal, it is logic. When it is restricted to definite objects of the understanding, it is metaphysics.

In this way the idea arises of a twofold metaphysics — a metaphysics of nature and a metaphysics of morals. Physics will therefore have an empirical part and a rational part. The same holds for ethics; but here the empirical part might be given the special name of practical anthropology, while the name morality is reserved for the rational part.

All trades, arts, and crafts have benefited from the division of labour. Instead of one person doing everything, each focuses on a specific kind of work, distinct from the rest in the skills it demands, so that he can do it more easily and to a higher standard. Where the different kinds of work are not separated, where everyone is a jack-of-all-trades, manufacturing remains at the most primitive level. It might be worth asking whether pure philosophy in all its branches doesn't require someone specifically dedicated to it. Would the whole enterprise of science benefit if those who like to mix the rational and empirical together in proportions unknown even to themselves — people who, to please public taste, call themselves independent thinkers and dismiss as nitpickers those who focus only on the rational part — were warned off trying to do two jobs at once that demand very different methods, each perhaps requiring its own special talent, and which combined in one person only produce bunglers? But here I only ask whether the nature of science doesn't require us to keep the empirical and the rational strictly separate, and to prefix to physics proper (or empirical physics) a metaphysics of nature, and to practical anthropology a metaphysics of morals. The metaphysics of morals must be cleared of everything empirical, so that we can see how much pure reason can accomplish in both cases, and from what sources it draws its a priori teaching. This inquiry must be undertaken either by all moralists (whose name is legion) or by some who feel a calling for it.

Since my concern here is moral philosophy, I narrow the question to this: is it not of the utmost importance to construct a pure moral philosophy that is completely cleared of everything empirical and belongs to anthropology? That such a philosophy must be possible is obvious from the common idea of duty and the moral law. Everyone must admit that if a law is to have moral force — that is, to be the basis of an obligation — it must carry absolute necessity with it. The command "Thou shalt not lie," for example, is not valid for human beings alone, as though other rational beings could ignore it. The same goes for all genuine moral laws. The basis of obligation, therefore, must not be sought in the nature of human beings or in the circumstances of the world they find themselves in, but a priori in the conception of pure reason alone. Any other precept founded on principles of mere experience may be universal in certain respects, but to the extent that it rests in the least on empirical grounds — even just for its motive — it can be a practical rule but never a moral law.

So not only are moral laws and their principles essentially distinguished from every other kind of practical knowledge with anything empirical in it; all moral philosophy rests entirely on its pure part. When applied to a human being, it borrows nothing whatever from knowledge of the human being himself (anthropology) but gives a priori laws to him as a rational being. These laws do require a judgement sharpened by experience — first, to know in what cases they apply, and second, to gain access to the human will and effective influence on conduct. Human beings are pulled by so many inclinations that, although capable of the idea of a practical pure reason, they are not so easily able to make it effective in their lives.

A metaphysics of morals is therefore indispensably necessary, not merely for speculative reasons — to investigate the sources of the practical principles found a priori in our reason — but also because morals themselves are liable to all kinds of corruption as long as we lack the guiding thread and supreme standard by which to estimate them correctly. For an action to be morally good, it is not enough that it conforms to the moral law; it must also be done for the sake of the law. Otherwise the conformity is only contingent and uncertain, since a non-moral principle, although it may sometimes produce actions that conform to the law, will also often produce actions that contradict it. Now it is only in a pure philosophy that we can look for the moral law in its purity and authenticity — and in a practical matter this is of the highest importance. We must therefore begin with pure philosophy (metaphysics), and without it there can be no moral philosophy at all. What mixes pure principles with empirical ones doesn't deserve the name of philosophy, for what distinguishes philosophy from common rational knowledge is that philosophy treats in separate sciences what common knowledge grasps only confusedly. Still less does it deserve the name of moral philosophy, since by this confusion it actually spoils the purity of morals themselves and works against its own end.

Let it not be thought that what is demanded here is already present in the propaedeutic that the celebrated Wolf prefixed to his moral philosophy — namely, his so-called general practical philosophy — and that we therefore have no entirely new field to enter. Just because it was meant as a general practical philosophy, it did not consider any particular kind of will — say, one determined solely from a priori principles without any empirical motives, which we might call a pure will. It considered volition in general, with all the actions and conditions that fall under that general heading. This is what distinguishes it from a metaphysics of morals, just as general logic, which treats the acts and rules of thought in general, is distinguished from transcendental philosophy, which treats the particular acts and rules of pure thought — that is, thought whose cognitions are wholly a priori. The metaphysics of morals has to examine the idea and the principles of a possible pure will, not the acts and conditions of human volition generally, which are largely drawn from psychology. It is true that the general moral philosophy talks about moral laws and duty (contrary to all fitness). But this is no objection, for in this respect too those authors stay true to their idea of the subject. They do not distinguish the motives prescribed by reason alone, wholly a priori — which are properly moral — from the empirical motives that the understanding raises to general concepts merely by comparing experiences. Without noticing the difference of their sources and treating them all as homogeneous, they consider only their greater or lesser quantity. This is how they frame their notion of obligation, which, though anything but moral, is all that can be achieved in a philosophy that passes no judgement at all on the origin of all possible practical concepts — whether they are a priori or only a posteriori.

Since I intend to publish a metaphysics of morals later, I am issuing these Fundamental Principles first. There is properly no foundation for a metaphysics of morals other than the critical examination of a pure practical reason — just as the foundation of metaphysics is the critical examination of pure speculative reason, already published. But first, the critical examination of pure practical reason is not so absolutely necessary as that of speculative reason, because in moral matters human reason can easily be brought to a high degree of correctness and completeness, even in the commonest understanding, whereas in its theoretical but pure use it is wholly dialectical. Second, if the critique of a pure practical reason is to be complete, it must also be possible to show its identity with speculative reason in a common principle, since ultimately there can be only one and the same reason, distinguished merely in its application. I could not, however, bring it to that completeness here without introducing considerations of a wholly different kind that would only confuse the reader. For this reason I have called this work Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysics of Morals rather than a Critical Examination of Pure Practical Reason.

Third, since a metaphysics of morals — despite its discouraging title — is capable of being presented in popular form, adapted to ordinary understanding, I find it useful to separate from it this preliminary treatise on its fundamental principles. That way I won't need to drag these unavoidably subtle discussions into a book of a simpler character.

The present treatise is nothing more than the investigation and establishment of the supreme principle of morality. This alone constitutes a study complete in itself, one that should be kept apart from every other moral investigation. My conclusions on this weighty question, which has so far been very unsatisfactorily examined, would no doubt gain considerable support from applying the same principle to the whole system, and would be greatly confirmed by the way it would prove adequate throughout. But I must forgo this advantage, which would after all be more gratifying than useful. The easy applicability of a principle and its apparent adequacy give no really certain proof of its soundness; they tend rather to inspire a partiality that prevents us from examining and estimating it strictly in itself, without regard to consequences.

In this work I have adopted the method I think most suitable, proceeding analytically from common knowledge to the determination of its ultimate principle, and then descending synthetically from the examination of this principle and its sources back to the common knowledge in which we find it employed. The division will therefore be as follows:
1 FIRST SECTION. Transition from the common rational knowledge of morality to the philosophical.
2 SECOND SECTION. Transition from popular moral philosophy to the metaphysics of morals.
3 THIRD SECTION. Final step from the metaphysics of morals to the critique of pure practical reason.

chapters.title: Section I — Transition from Common Rational Knowledge of Morals to Philosophical Knowledge of Morals
paragraphs: Nothing in the world — or even outside it — can possibly be conceived as good without qualification, except a good will. Intelligence, wit, judgement, and the other talents of the mind, whatever we call them, or courage, resolution, perseverance, as qualities of temperament, are undoubtedly good and desirable in many ways. But these gifts of nature can also become extremely bad and harmful if the will that uses them — the will that constitutes what we call character — is not good. The same goes for the gifts of fortune. Power, wealth, honour, even health, and the general well-being and contentment with one's condition that we call happiness, inspire pride and often presumption, unless there is a good will to correct their influence on the mind and so to rectify the whole principle of acting and adapt it to its end. The sight of a being not adorned with a single trace of a pure and good will, enjoying unbroken prosperity, can never give pleasure to an impartial rational spectator. A good will, then, seems to be the indispensable condition even of being worthy of happiness.

There are some qualities that are useful to this good will itself and may make its work easier, yet have no intrinsic unconditional value, but always presuppose a good will, which limits the esteem we rightly have for them and forbids us to regard them as absolutely good. Moderation in the affections and passions, self-control, and calm deliberation are not only good in many ways but even seem to be part of the intrinsic worth of the person. Yet they are far from deserving to be called good without qualification, although the ancients praised them unconditionally. Without the principles of a good will, they can become extremely bad: the coolness of a villain not only makes him far more dangerous, but also makes him directly more abominable in our eyes than he would have been without it.

A good will is good not because of what it brings about or accomplishes, not because of its fitness for attaining some proposed end, but simply by virtue of the act of willing. That is, it is good in itself, and considered by itself it is to be esteemed far higher than anything that could be produced by it in favour of any inclination — or even the sum total of all inclinations. Even if, by some special misfortune or the stingy provision of a step-motherly nature, this will should completely lack the power to accomplish its purpose; even if with its greatest efforts it should achieve nothing, and there remained only the good will (not, of course, a mere wish, but the summoning of every means in our power) — then, like a jewel, it would still shine by its own light, as something that has its whole value in itself. Its usefulness or fruitlessness can neither add to nor take away from this value. Usefulness would be, as it were, only the setting that lets us handle the jewel more easily in everyday commerce, or that draws the attention of those who are not yet connoisseurs. It cannot recommend the jewel to true connoisseurs or determine its value.

There is, however, something so strange in this idea of the absolute value of the mere will — an idea that takes no account of utility — that, despite the full agreement of even common reason with it, a suspicion must arise that this idea may really be the product of mere high-flown fancy, and that we may have misunderstood nature's purpose in giving reason as the governor of our will. We will therefore examine this idea from that point of view.

In the physical constitution of an organized being — that is, a being adapted suitably to the purposes of life — we take it as a fundamental principle that no organ for any purpose will be found except the one best suited and adapted for that purpose. Now in a being that has reason and a will, if the proper object of nature were its conservation, its welfare — in a word, its happiness — then nature would have made a very bad arrangement in selecting the creature's reason to carry out this purpose. All the actions the creature has to perform with this purpose in view, and the whole rule of its conduct, would have been far more surely prescribed to it by instinct, and that end would have been attained much more reliably than reason could ever achieve. If reason had been given to this favoured creature on top of instinct, it should only have served to contemplate the happy constitution of its nature, to admire it, to congratulate itself on it, and to feel thankful for it to the beneficent cause — not to subject its desires to that weak and delusive guidance and meddle bunglingly with nature's purpose. In a word, nature would have made sure that reason did not break out into practical exercise, nor presume, with its weak insight, to think out for itself the plan of happiness and the means of attaining it. Nature would have taken on herself the choice not only of the ends but also of the means, and with wise foresight would have entrusted both to instinct.

And in fact we find that the more a cultivated reason applies itself with deliberate purpose to the enjoyment of life and happiness, the further the person falls short of true satisfaction. From this circumstance there arises in many — if they are honest enough to admit it — a certain degree of misology, that is, hatred of reason, especially in those most experienced in its use. After calculating all the advantages they derive — I won't say from the invention of all the arts of common luxury, but even from the sciences (which seem to them after all only a luxury of the understanding) — they find they have actually only brought more trouble on their shoulders rather than gained in happiness. They end by envying, rather than despising, the more ordinary type of people who stay closer to the guidance of mere instinct and don't allow reason much influence on their conduct. We must admit that the judgement of those who would very much lower the lofty praise of the advantages reason gives us with regard to the happiness and satisfaction of life, or who would even reduce them below zero, is by no means morose or ungrateful to the goodness with which the world is governed. At the root of those judgements lies the idea that our existence has a different and far nobler end, for which — and not for happiness — reason is properly intended, and which must therefore be regarded as the supreme condition to which the private ends of human beings must, for the most part, be subordinated.

For reason is not competent to guide the will with certainty regarding its objects and the satisfaction of all our needs (which it even multiplies to some extent); an implanted instinct would have led to that end with much greater certainty. Yet reason is nevertheless given to us as a practical faculty — that is, as one meant to have influence on the will. Granting that nature in distributing her capacities has adapted means to ends, the true destination of reason must be to produce a will not merely good as a means to something else, but good in itself. For this, reason was absolutely necessary. This will, although not the sole and complete good, must be the supreme good and the condition of every other, even of the desire for happiness. Under these circumstances, there is nothing inconsistent with the wisdom of nature in the fact that the cultivation of reason, required for the first and unconditional purpose, in many ways interferes — at least in this life — with the attainment of the second, which is always conditional, namely happiness. It may even reduce happiness to nothing, without nature thereby failing of her purpose. For reason recognizes the establishment of a good will as its highest practical destination, and in attaining this purpose is capable only of a satisfaction of its own kind — namely, that which comes from attaining an end determined by reason alone, even though this may involve many disappointments to the ends of inclination.

We now have to develop the notion of a will that deserves to be highly esteemed for itself and is good without a view to anything further — a notion that already exists in sound natural understanding, requiring rather to be clarified than taught, and which in estimating the value of our actions always takes the first place and constitutes the condition of all the rest. To do this, we will take the notion of duty, which includes that of a good will, although under certain subjective restrictions and hindrances. These, however, far from concealing the good will or making it unrecognizable, rather bring it out by contrast and make it shine all the brighter.

I leave aside here all actions already recognized as inconsistent with duty, even if they may be useful for this or that purpose. For with these, the question whether they are done from duty cannot arise at all, since they actually conflict with duty. I also set aside those actions that really do conform to duty, but which people have no direct inclination to perform, doing them only because they are driven to it by some other inclination. For in this case it is easy to tell whether the action that agrees with duty is done from duty or from a selfish motive. It is much harder to make this distinction when the action accords with duty and the subject also has a direct inclination to it. For example, it is always a duty for a shopkeeper not to overcharge an inexperienced customer; and wherever there is much commerce, the prudent merchant does not overcharge but keeps a fixed price for everyone, so that a child can buy from him just as well as anyone else. People are honestly served this way. But this is not enough to make us believe the shopkeeper acted from duty and from principles of honesty: his own advantage required it. It is out of the question in this case to suppose he might in addition have a direct inclination in favour of his customers, so that out of love he gave no one an advantage over another. Accordingly the action was done neither from duty nor from direct inclination, but merely from a selfish motive.

On the other hand, it is a duty to preserve one's life, and in addition everyone has a direct inclination to do so. But on that account the often anxious care most people take for their lives has no intrinsic worth, and their maxim has no moral import. They preserve their life as duty requires, no doubt, but not because duty requires it. On the other hand, if adversity and hopeless sorrow have completely killed the relish for life; if the unfortunate person, strong in mind, indignant at his fate rather than despondent or dejected, wishes for death, and yet preserves his life without loving it — not from inclination or fear, but from duty — then his maxim has a moral worth.

It is a duty to be kind to others when we can. Beyond this, there are many people so sympathetically constituted that, without any motive of vanity or self-interest, they find pleasure in spreading joy around them and can delight in the satisfaction of others when it is their own work. But I maintain that in such a case an action of this kind, however appropriate and amiable it may be, still has no true moral worth. It is on a level with other inclinations — for example, the inclination to honour, which, if it happens to be directed to what is in fact of public utility and consistent with duty and therefore honourable, deserves praise and encouragement, but not esteem. The maxim lacks the moral import — namely, that such actions be done from duty, not from inclination. Suppose the mind of that philanthropist were clouded by his own sorrow, extinguishing all sympathy with the lot of others, and that, while he still has the power to help others in distress, he is not touched by their trouble because he is absorbed with his own. Now suppose he tears himself out of this dead insensibility and performs the action without any inclination to it, but simply from duty — then for the first time his action has its genuine moral worth. Further still: if nature has put little sympathy in the heart of this or that person; if he, an upright man by hypothesis, is by temperament cold and indifferent to the sufferings of others, perhaps because in respect of his own he is provided with the special gift of patience and fortitude, and supposes — or even demands — that others should have the same; and such a person would certainly not be the lowest product of nature — but if nature had not specially fitted him to be a philanthropist, would he not still find in himself a source from which to give himself a far higher worth than that of a good-natured temperament? Unquestionably. It is precisely in this that the moral worth of the character is brought out, which is incomparably the highest of all: that he is kind not from inclination, but from duty.

To secure one's own happiness is a duty, at least indirectly; for discontent with one's condition, under the pressure of many anxieties and amidst unsatisfied wants, might easily become a great temptation to violate duty. But here again, without looking to duty, all human beings already have the strongest and most intimate inclination to happiness, because it is in this very idea that all inclinations are combined into one total. The precept of happiness is, however, often of such a sort that it greatly interferes with some inclinations, and yet a person cannot form any definite and certain conception of the sum of satisfaction of all of them, which is called happiness. It is not surprising, then, that a single inclination, definite as to what it promises and as to the time within which it can be gratified, can often overcome such a fluctuating idea. A gouty patient, for instance, can choose to enjoy what he likes and to suffer what he may, since on his calculation he has at least on this occasion not sacrificed the enjoyment of the present moment to a possibly mistaken expectation of a happiness that is supposed to lie in health. But even in this case, if the general desire for happiness did not influence his will, and supposing that in his particular case health was not a necessary element in this calculation, there yet remains in this case — as in all others — this law: that he should promote his happiness not from inclination but from duty. By this his conduct would first acquire true moral worth.

It is undoubtedly in this manner that we are to understand those passages of Scripture in which we are commanded to love our neighbour, even our enemy. For love, as an affection, cannot be commanded; but kindness for duty's sake can be — even when we are not impelled to it by any inclination, indeed are repelled by a natural and unconquerable aversion. This is practical love, not pathological love — a love seated in the will and not in the propensities of sense, in principles of action and not of tender sympathy. And it is this love alone which can be commanded.

The second proposition is: an action done from duty derives its moral worth not from the purpose to be attained by it, but from the maxim by which it is determined. It therefore does not depend on the realization of the object of the action, but only on the principle of volition by which the action takes place, regardless of any object of desire. It is clear from what precedes that the purposes we may have in view in our actions, or their effects regarded as ends and springs of the will, cannot give actions any unconditional or moral worth. In what, then, can their worth lie, if it is not to consist in the will in relation to its expected effect? It cannot lie anywhere but in the principle of the will, regardless of the ends that can be attained by the action. For the will stands, as it were, between its a priori principle, which is formal, and its a posteriori spring, which is material — as between two roads. It must be determined by something; so when an action is done from duty, it must be determined by the formal principle of volition, every material principle having been withdrawn from it.

The third proposition, which is a consequence of the two preceding ones, I would express like this: duty is the necessity of acting from respect for the law. I may have inclination for an object as the effect of my proposed action, but I cannot have respect for it, just because it is an effect and not an energy of will. Similarly I cannot have respect for inclination, whether my own or someone else's. At most, if it is my own, I can approve of it; if it is another's, I can sometimes even love it — that is, look on it as favourable to my own interest. Only what is connected with my will as a principle, in no way as an effect — what does not subserve my inclination but overpowers it, or at least excludes it from the calculation in the case of choice — in other words, simply the law itself, can be an object of respect, and so a command. Now an action done from duty must wholly exclude the influence of inclination and with it every object of the will, so that nothing remains that can determine the will except, objectively, the law, and subjectively, pure respect for this practical law. The maxim* that follows is that I should follow this law even at the cost of thwarting all my inclinations.

* A maxim is the subjective principle of volition. The objective principle (the one that would also serve subjectively as a practical principle for all rational beings if reason had full power over the faculty of desire) is the practical law.

Thus the moral worth of an action does not lie in the effect expected from it, nor in any principle of action that has to borrow its motive from this expected effect. For all these effects — agreeableness of one's condition and even the promotion of the happiness of others — could have been brought about by other causes too, so that the will of a rational being would not be needed for them. Yet it is in the will alone that the supreme and unconditional good can be found. The pre-eminent good we call moral can therefore consist in nothing but the conception of law in itself, which is of course only possible in a rational being, insofar as this conception, and not the expected effect, determines the will. This is a good already present in the person who acts accordingly, and we do not have to wait for it to appear first in the result. *

* It might be objected here that I take refuge behind the word "respect" in an obscure feeling, instead of giving a distinct solution of the question by a concept of reason. But although respect is a feeling, it is not a feeling received through influence; it is self-produced by a rational concept, and is therefore specifically distinct from all feelings of the former kind, which may be referred to either inclination or fear. What I recognize immediately as a law for me, I recognize with respect. This merely signifies the consciousness that my will is subordinate to a law, without the intervention of other influences on my sense. The immediate determination of the will by the law, and the consciousness of this, is called respect, so that it is regarded as an effect of the law on the subject, not as its cause. Respect is properly the conception of a worth that thwarts my self-love. Accordingly it is something considered neither as an object of inclination nor of fear, although it has something analogous to both. The object of respect is the law alone — the law we impose on ourselves and yet recognize as necessary in itself. As a law, we are subjected to it without consulting self-love; as imposed by us on ourselves, it is a result of our will. In the former aspect it has an analogy to fear, in the latter to inclination. Respect for a person is properly only respect for the law (of honesty, etc.) of which he gives us an example. Since we also regard the improvement of our talents as a duty, we consider that we see in a person of talent, as it were, the example of a law (namely, to become like him in this by practice), and this constitutes our respect. All so-called moral interest consists simply in respect for the law.

But what sort of law can that be, the conception of which must determine the will, even without paying any regard to the effect expected from it, in order that this will may be called good absolutely and without qualification? Since I have deprived the will of every impulse that could arise from obedience to any particular law, there remains nothing but the universal conformity of its actions to law in general, which alone is to serve the will as a principle. That is: I am never to act otherwise than so that I could also will that my maxim should become a universal law. Here it is the simple conformity to law in general — without assuming any particular law applicable to certain actions — that serves the will as its principle, and must serve it so, if duty is not to be an empty delusion and a chimerical notion. The common reason of human beings in its practical judgements coincides perfectly with this and always has in view the principle here suggested. Take for example this question: may I, when in distress, make a promise with the intention of not keeping it? I readily distinguish two senses the question may have: is it prudent, or is it right, to make a false promise? The first may undoubtedly often be the case. I see clearly that it is not enough to extricate myself from a present difficulty by means of this subterfuge; I have to weigh whether much greater inconvenience may not in future spring from this lie than from the trouble I now escape. With all my supposed cunning, the consequences cannot be foreseen so easily but that credit once lost may be far more damaging to me than any mischief I now try to avoid. So I should consider whether it would not be more prudent to act on a universal maxim and make it a habit to promise nothing except with the intention of keeping it. But it soon becomes clear that such a maxim would still rest only on the fear of consequences. Now it is wholly different to be truthful from duty and to be truthful from fear of bad consequences. In the first case, the very notion of the action already implies a law for me; in the second, I must first look around for the results that might affect me. For to deviate from the principle of duty is beyond doubt wicked; but to be unfaithful to my maxim of prudence may often be very advantageous to me, although sticking to it is certainly safer. The shortest, and an unerring, way to discover the answer to the question whether a lying promise is consistent with duty is to ask myself: "Would I be content that my maxim (to extricate myself from difficulty by a false promise) should hold good as a universal law, for myself as well as for others?" Could I say to myself: "Anyone may make a deceitful promise when he finds himself in a difficulty he cannot otherwise escape"? I quickly become aware that while I can will the lie, I cannot by any means will that lying should be a universal law. For with such a law there would be no promises at all, since it would be useless to declare my intention regarding future actions to people who would not believe my declaration, or who, if they hastily did believe it, would pay me back in my own coin. Hence my maxim, as soon as it should be made a universal law, would necessarily destroy itself.

I therefore do not need any far-reaching penetration to discern what I have to do in order that my will may be morally good. Inexperienced in the course of the world, incapable of being prepared for all its contingencies, I only ask myself: can you also will that your maxim should be a universal law? If not, then it must be rejected — not because of any disadvantage it might bring me or even others, but because it cannot enter as a principle into a possible universal legislation, and reason extorts from me immediate respect for such legislation. I do not yet discern on what this respect is based (the philosopher may inquire into that), but at least I understand that it is an estimation of the worth that far outweighs all the worth of what is recommended by inclination, and that the necessity of acting from pure respect for the practical law is what constitutes duty, to which every other motive must give way, because it is the condition of a will being good in itself, and the worth of such a will is above everything.

Thus, without leaving the moral knowledge of common human reason, we have arrived at its principle. Ordinary people do not, of course, conceive it in such an abstract and universal form, but they always have it really before their eyes and use it as the standard of their decisions. It would be easy to show how, with this compass in hand, people are well able to distinguish in every case what is good or bad, consistent with duty or not — if, without teaching them anything new, we only, like Socrates, direct their attention to the principle they themselves employ. So we don't need science and philosophy to know what to do in order to be honest and good, or even wise and virtuous. We might have guessed in advance that the knowledge of what every person is bound to do, and therefore also to know, would be within reach of every person, even the most ordinary. We cannot help admiring the great advantage that the practical judgement has over the theoretical in common human understanding. In the theoretical sphere, if common reason ventures to depart from the laws of experience and the perceptions of the senses, it falls into mere inconceivabilities and self-contradictions, or at least into a chaos of uncertainty, obscurity, and instability. But in the practical sphere, it is precisely when common understanding excludes all sensible springs from practical laws that its power of judgement begins to show to advantage. It then even becomes subtle, whether it is splitting hairs with its own conscience or with other claims about what should be called right, or whether it wants to determine honestly, for its own instruction, the worth of actions. In the latter case it may have as good a hope of hitting the mark as any philosopher whatever. Indeed it is almost more sure of doing so, because the philosopher can have no other principle, yet may easily confuse his judgement by a multitude of considerations foreign to the matter, and so turn aside from the right way. Would it not therefore be wiser in moral matters to acquiesce in the judgement of common reason, or at most to call in philosophy only to make the system of morals more complete and intelligible and its rules more convenient for use (especially for disputation) — but not to draw the common understanding away from its happy simplicity, or lead it by means of philosophy into a new path of inquiry and instruction?

Innocence is indeed a glorious thing, but on the other hand it is very sad that it cannot well maintain itself and is easily seduced. On that account even wisdom — which otherwise consists more in conduct than in knowledge — needs science, not in order to learn from it, but to secure for its precepts admission and permanence. Against all the commands of duty that reason presents to a person as so worthy of respect, he feels in himself a powerful counterweight in his wants and inclinations, the complete satisfaction of which he sums up under the name of happiness. Reason issues its commands unyieldingly, without promising anything to the inclinations, and as it were with disregard and contempt for their claims, which are so impetuous and at the same time so plausible, and which will not allow themselves to be suppressed by any command. Hence there arises a natural dialectic — that is, a disposition to argue against these strict laws of duty and to question their validity, or at least their purity and strictness; and, if possible, to bring them more into line with our wishes and inclinations — in other words, to corrupt them at their very source and entirely destroy their worth, a thing that even common practical reason cannot ultimately call good.

In this way the common reason of human beings is compelled to step outside its sphere and take a step into the field of a practical philosophy — not to satisfy any speculative need (which never occurs to it so long as it is content to be mere sound reason), but on practical grounds, to obtain information and clear instruction about the source of its principle and the correct determination of it against the maxims based on wants and inclinations. This way it can escape from the perplexity of opposing claims and not run the risk of losing all genuine moral principles through the ambiguity into which it easily falls. So when practical reason cultivates itself, there imperceptibly arises in it a dialectic that forces it to seek help in philosophy, just as happens to it in its theoretical use; and in this case, as in the other, it will find rest nowhere except in a thorough critical examination of our reason.

chapters.title: Section II — Transition from Popular Moral Philosophy to the Metaphysics of Morals
paragraphs: Although we have so far derived our concept of duty from the ordinary exercise of practical reason, this certainly does not mean that we have treated it as an empirical concept. On the contrary, experience of human conduct repeatedly gives rise to complaints, which we ourselves admit are justified, that no certain instance of a disposition to act from pure duty can be found. Many actions conform to what duty commands; whether they are performed strictly from duty, and therefore possess moral worth, always remains doubtful. That is why philosophers in every age have denied that such a disposition exists in human actions at all, explaining everything through a more or less refined self-love. They did not thereby question the validity of the concept of morality. Rather, they sincerely deplored the weakness and corruption of human nature. It is noble enough to adopt as its rule an idea deserving such respect, yet too weak to follow it. Reason, which ought to provide its law, is employed merely to serve the inclinations, either separately or, at best, in the greatest possible harmony with one another.

Experience can never establish with complete certainty even a single case in which an action’s maxim, however right the action itself may be, rested solely on moral grounds and the concept of duty. Sometimes the most searching self-examination reveals nothing except duty’s moral principle that could have moved us to a particular action or so great a sacrifice. Even then, we cannot infer with certainty that the will was not actually determined by some hidden impulse of self-love masquerading as duty. We gladly flatter ourselves by claiming credit for a nobler motive. In reality, however rigorously we examine ourselves, we can never fully penetrate the hidden sources of action. When moral worth is at issue, our concern is not with the actions we can see, but with their inner principles, which remain unseen.

Moreover, nothing could better serve those who ridicule morality as a mere fantasy of a vain imagination overreaching itself than to concede that concepts of duty must be drawn exclusively from experience. People lazily suppose the same about all other concepts; to grant it here would assure morality’s opponents a victory. From love of humanity, I am willing to admit that most of our actions are indeed correct. Look more closely, however, and everywhere the beloved self steps prominently forward: it is the self those actions serve, rather than duty’s strict command, which would often demand self-denial. One need not be an enemy of virtue to doubt at times whether true virtue exists anywhere in the world. A dispassionate observer, who does not mistake even an ardent wish for goodness for its reality, may have such doubts, especially as advancing years make judgement partly wiser through experience and partly sharper in observation. Only one conviction can then keep us from abandoning our ideas of duty altogether and sustain a well-founded respect for its law in the soul. Even if no action had ever arisen from such pure sources, the question is not what does or does not happen: reason itself, independently of experience, prescribes what ought to happen. It therefore uncompromisingly commands actions of which the world may never have furnished an example, whose very possibility someone relying entirely on experience might seriously doubt. For example, even if no sincere friend had ever existed, pure sincerity in friendship would still be required of everyone. Before all experience, this duty is already contained, as duty, in the idea of reason determining the will through a priori principles.

We must add a further point. Unless we deny that the concept of morality has any truth or relates to any possible object, we must admit that its law applies to every rational creature, not merely to human beings. It holds with absolute necessity, rather than under contingent conditions or subject to exceptions. Clearly, no experience could allow us to infer even the possibility of such apodeictic laws. By what right could we demand unlimited respect for a universal command addressed to every rational nature if it perhaps holds only under humanity’s contingent conditions? How could laws determining our will count as laws determining the will of rational beings generally—and apply to us only as such beings—if they were merely empirical, instead of originating entirely a priori in pure but practical reason?

Nothing could be more disastrous for morality than the attempt to derive it from examples. Every example offered to me must itself first be tested against moral principles to establish whether it deserves to serve as an original example, a pattern. It can never provide the concept of morality on its own authority. Even the Holy One of the Gospels must first be measured against our ideal of moral perfection before we can recognise Him as such. Thus He says of Himself, "Why call ye Me (whom you see) good; none is good (the model of good) but God only (whom ye do not see)?" But where do we obtain the concept of God as the supreme good? Solely from the idea of moral perfection, formed a priori by reason and inseparably joined to the concept of a free will. Imitation has no place in morality. Examples can only encourage us: they remove doubt that the law’s commands can be fulfilled and make visible what the practical rule expresses in more general terms. They never entitle us to abandon the true original, which lies in reason, and take examples as our guide instead.

If, then, every genuine supreme principle of morality must rest solely on pure reason, independently of all experience, I scarcely think we need ask whether these concepts should be presented in their generality, in abstracto, as established a priori together with their corresponding principles. We must do so if our knowledge is to differ from ordinary knowledge and deserve to be called philosophical.

In our own day, however, perhaps the question does need asking. Were we to take a vote on the choice between pure rational knowledge separated from everything empirical—that is, a metaphysics of morals—and popular practical philosophy, it is easy to guess which side would win.

Coming down to popular concepts is certainly admirable, provided we have first successfully climbed to the principles of pure reason. We must establish ethics on metaphysics first; once it stands securely, we can gain it a hearing by presenting it popularly. But aiming at popularity in the initial investigation, on which the validity of the principles depends, is altogether absurd. It cannot claim the very rare merit of genuine philosophical accessibility: being understandable requires no art when one abandons every effort at thorough insight. Worse, it produces a repellent jumble of collected observations and principles only half thought through. Shallow minds enjoy this because it supplies material for everyday conversation. Discerning minds find only confusion; dissatisfied and unable to find their way, they turn away. Meanwhile, philosophers who see through the illusion receive little attention when they ask people to leave this counterfeit popularity behind for a time, so that, after gaining definite insight, they can become genuinely accessible.

Look at moralists’ efforts in this fashionable style. We find a wonderful mixture: now the special constitution of human nature, though including the idea of rational nature generally; now perfection, now happiness; moral sense here, fear of God there; a little of this and a little of that. They never think to ask whether the principles of morality belong in the study of human nature at all, a study available to us only through experience. If they do not—if these principles are found wholly a priori, free of everything empirical, solely in pure rational concepts, and nowhere else in even the slightest degree—then we should investigate them separately. We should undertake pure practical philosophy, or, to use a much-disparaged name, a metaphysics of morals, * complete this inquiry on its own terms, and ask the public seeking a popular treatment to wait for its results.

* Just as we distinguish pure mathematics from applied mathematics, and pure logic from applied logic, we may distinguish pure moral philosophy, or metaphysics, from moral philosophy applied to human nature. This terminology immediately reminds us that moral principles do not rest on features of human nature. They must stand a priori on their own, while allowing practical rules to be derived from them for every rational nature, and therefore for human nature as well.

Such a metaphysics of morals must stand entirely apart from anthropology, theology, physics, and hyperphysics, and even more from occult qualities, which we might call hypophysical. It is not merely the indispensable foundation of all sound theoretical knowledge of duties; it is also urgently needed if their commands are actually to be fulfilled. The pure concept of duty, free from any foreign admixture of empirical attractions—in a word, the concept of the moral law—acts on the human heart through reason alone. Reason then first recognises that it can be practical by itself. This influence is so much stronger than every other motive * drawn from experience that, conscious of its own worth, it disdains those motives and can gradually master them. Mixed ethics, by contrast, combines motives from feelings and inclinations with rational concepts. It leaves the mind wavering between motives that cannot be brought under a single principle, that produce good only accidentally, and that very often produce evil.

* I have a letter from the late, admirable Sulzer asking why moral instruction achieves so little although it contains so much that convinces reason. I delayed my reply to make it complete, but the answer is simply this: the teachers have not clarified their own concepts. Trying to compensate by gathering motives for moral goodness from every direction, they make their medicine stronger only to spoil it. Even ordinary understanding can see the difference. Imagine, on one side, an honest act performed with firm resolve, without any thought of advantage in this world or another, despite the strongest temptations of need or enticement. On the other side, imagine a similar act influenced, however slightly, by a foreign motive. The first leaves the second far behind and eclipses it, elevating the soul and inspiring a wish to act the same way oneself. Even fairly young children feel this impression. Duties should never be presented to them in any other light.

What we have said so far makes several points clear. Every moral concept has its seat and origin entirely a priori in reason, as much in the most ordinary reason as in the most speculative. Such concepts cannot be abstracted from empirical knowledge, which is always contingent. Their pure origin alone qualifies them to serve as our supreme practical principle: the more empirical material we add, the more we diminish their authentic influence and the absolute value of actions. Deriving these concepts and laws from pure reason, presenting them without admixture, and determining the full scope of this practical or pure rational knowledge—the entire faculty of pure practical reason—is therefore indispensable to speculation and of the greatest practical importance. We must not make its principles depend on the particular character of human reason, although speculative philosophy may permit or sometimes even require that. Moral laws must apply to every rational creature, so we must derive them from the general concept of a rational being. Morality does need anthropology when applied to human beings. Initially, however, we must treat it independently as pure philosophy, as a metaphysics complete in itself; in such clearly distinct branches of science, this is readily done. Without possessing this metaphysics, we could neither determine the moral element of duty in right actions for speculative criticism nor establish morality on genuine principles even for ordinary practical purposes. This matters especially for moral instruction, if it is to produce pure moral dispositions, implant them in people’s minds, and promote the greatest possible good in the world.

Our inquiry must do more than follow the natural steps already taken from ordinary moral judgement—which here deserves great respect—to philosophical judgement. It must also advance from a popular philosophy that can only grope forward with examples to metaphysics. Metaphysics allows itself to be checked by empirical considerations and, since it must measure the entire scope of this rational knowledge, extends to ideal concepts where even examples fail us. To accomplish that advance, we must trace and clearly describe reason’s practical faculty, starting with the general rules determining it and continuing to the point where the concept of duty arises from it.

Everything in nature operates according to laws. Only a rational being can act according to the conception of laws, that is, according to principles; only such a being has a will. Deriving actions from principles requires reason, so the will is simply practical reason. If reason unfailingly determines the will, actions recognised as objectively necessary are also subjectively necessary for that being. The will then chooses only what reason, independently of inclination, recognises as practically necessary, or good. But suppose reason alone does not sufficiently determine the will, which is also subject to subjective conditions, particular impulses, that do not always agree with objective conditions. In short, suppose the will does not completely accord with reason, as is actually the case with human beings. Actions recognised as objectively necessary are then subjectively contingent, and determining such a will through objective laws is obligation. That is, we conceive the relation between objective laws and a will that is not thoroughly good as the determination of a rational being’s will by rational principles which, given its nature, the will does not necessarily follow.
An objective principle, conceived as binding on a will, is called a command of reason. The formula expressing that command is called an imperative.

Every imperative uses the word ought [or shall], thereby expressing the relation between an objective law of reason and a will whose subjective constitution does not necessarily make it follow that law: an obligation. Imperatives say that doing or refraining from something would be good, but address a will that does not invariably act merely because it conceives an action as good. What is practically good determines the will through rational concepts, and therefore objectively rather than through subjective causes: through principles valid for every rational being as such. This differs from the pleasant, which influences the will only through sensation, on merely subjective grounds valid for the sensibility of this or that individual, rather than as a rational principle holding for everyone. *

* When desires depend on sensations, we call this inclination, which therefore always signifies a lack. When a will capable of being contingently determined depends on rational principles, we call this an interest. Interest occurs only in a dependent will that does not always conform to reason by itself; we cannot conceive of any interest in the Divine will. Yet the human will can take an interest in something without acting from interest. The first means practical interest in the action; the second, pathological interest in the action’s object. The first concerns the will’s dependence solely on rational principles in themselves. The second concerns dependence on rational principles for the sake of inclination, with reason merely supplying practical rules for satisfying that inclination. In the first case, the action interests me; in the second, its object interests me because it pleases me. As we saw in the first section, an action done from duty directs our attention not to interest in its object, but solely to interest in the action itself and its rational principle, the law.

A perfectly good will would likewise be subject to objective laws, the laws of good. Yet we could not conceive it as obliged by them to act lawfully, because its own subjective constitution permits it to be determined only by the concept of good. No imperatives therefore apply to the Divine will or, generally, to a holy will. Ought has no place here: willing is already necessarily in accord with the law of its own accord. Imperatives are thus merely formulas expressing how the objective laws of all willing relate to the subjective imperfection of a particular rational being’s will—for example, the human will.

Every imperative commands either hypothetically or categorically. A hypothetical imperative presents a possible action as practically necessary as a means to something else that is willed, or at least might possibly be willed. A categorical imperative would present an action as necessary in itself, without reference to a further end: as objectively necessary.

Every practical law presents a possible action as good and therefore necessary for a subject whose practical conduct can be determined by reason. All imperatives are consequently formulas determining an action that is necessary according to the principle of a will good in some respect. If an action is good only as a means to something else, the imperative is hypothetical. If it is conceived as good in itself, and therefore necessarily as the principle of a will that conforms to reason of itself, the imperative is categorical.

The imperative thus tells me which action within my power would be good. It presents a practical rule to a will that does not immediately perform an action simply because it is good: either the subject does not always know its goodness, or, even when it knows, its maxims may conflict with the objective principles of practical reason.

A hypothetical imperative therefore says only that an action is good for a possible or actual purpose. For a possible purpose it is a problematical practical principle; for an actual one, an assertorial practical principle. The categorical imperative declares an action objectively necessary in itself, without reference to any purpose or further end, and holds as an apodeictic practical principle.

Anything possible only through a rational being’s power can also be conceived as a possible purpose of some will. Principles governing the means necessary for possible purposes are therefore infinitely numerous. Every science has a practical part: problems stating that some end is possible for us, and imperatives indicating how to reach it. These may generally be called imperatives of skill. Here we do not ask whether the end is rational or good, but only what must be done to achieve it. Instructions enabling a physician to restore a patient to full health and a poisoner to cause certain death have equal value in this respect: each perfectly accomplishes its purpose. Because early youth cannot tell us which ends we may adopt in life, parents arrange for their children to learn a great many things. They equip them to use means towards all sorts of arbitrary ends, none of which they can know will become the pupil’s aim, though any of them might. Their concern about this is so great that they commonly neglect to shape and correct the child’s judgement about the value of things that might be chosen as ends.

There is, however, one end we may assume all rational beings actually have, insofar as imperatives apply to them—that is, insofar as they are dependent beings. This purpose is not merely possible: natural necessity entitles us to assume with certainty that they all actually have it, and it is happiness. The hypothetical imperative expressing an action’s practical necessity as a means of advancing happiness is assertorial. We should not present the action as necessary for an uncertain, merely possible purpose, but for one we can presuppose with certainty and a priori in every human being, since it belongs to that being’s existence. Skill in choosing means to one’s own greatest well-being may be called prudence * in the narrowest sense. An imperative concerning the means to one’s own happiness, a precept of prudence, therefore always remains hypothetical. It commands the action only as a means to a further purpose, never absolutely.

* Prudence has two meanings. In one sense we may call it knowledge of the world; in the other, private prudence. The first is the ability to influence other people and use them for one’s own purposes. The second is the discernment to combine all those purposes for one’s lasting benefit. Ultimately, even the value of the first depends on the second. Someone prudent in the first sense but not the second would therefore be better described as clever and cunning, yet imprudent overall.

Finally, one imperative commands a particular course of conduct directly, without making it conditional on any further purpose to be achieved. This imperative is categorical. It concerns the action’s form and the principle producing it, rather than its content or intended result. What is essentially good lies in the disposition of mind, whatever consequences follow. We may call this the imperative of morality.

Willing according to these three kinds of principle also differs distinctly in the obligation imposed on the will. To mark this difference clearly, I think the best names, in their respective order, are rules of skill, counsels of prudence, and commands, or laws, of morality. Only law involves unconditional, objective necessity, and thus universal validity. Commands are laws that must be obeyed, followed even against inclination. Counsels too involve necessity, but only under a contingent subjective condition: they depend on whether a particular person includes this or that within his happiness. The categorical imperative, by contrast, has no limiting condition. Since it is absolutely, though practically, necessary, we may properly call it a command. We could also call the first kind of imperative technical, belonging to art; the second pragmatic, * belonging to welfare; and the third moral, belonging to free conduct generally, or to morals.

* This seems to me the most accurate definition of pragmatic in its proper sense. Sanctions are called pragmatic when they arise, not properly from the law of states as necessary enactments, but from precautions for general welfare. History is written pragmatically when it teaches prudence: when it instructs people how to provide for their interests better than, or at least as well as, people in earlier times.

We now face the question: how are these imperatives possible? We are not asking how to conceive the performance of the action an imperative commands, but only how to conceive the obligation of the will that it expresses. An imperative of skill needs no special explanation. Whoever wills an end also wills, insofar as reason governs his conduct, the indispensable means within his power. In respect of willing, this proposition is analytical. When I will an object as an effect I am to produce, I already conceive my own causality as an acting cause—that is, my use of means. The imperative draws the concept of the necessary actions from the concept of willing the end. Determining the means to a proposed end does require synthetical propositions, but these concern the object and its realisation, not the principle or the act of will. Mathematics, for example, teaches through synthetical propositions that to bisect a line by an infallible principle I must draw intersecting arcs from its endpoints. But once I know that only this procedure can perform the intended operation, the statement that fully willing the operation also means willing the required action is analytical. Conceiving something as an effect I can produce in a certain way and conceiving myself as acting that way are one and the same.

If giving a definite and consistent concept of happiness were equally easy, imperatives of prudence would exactly match those of skill and would likewise be analytical. In both cases we could say: "Whoever wills the end, wills also (according to the dictate of reason necessarily) the indispensable means thereto which are in his power." Unfortunately, happiness is so indefinite a concept that, although everyone wants it, no one can state definitely and consistently what he actually wishes and wills. Every element of happiness is wholly empirical, borrowed from experience; yet the idea of happiness requires an absolute whole, the greatest possible well-being in my present circumstances and all future ones. Even the most perceptive and powerful being, if finite, cannot form a definite concept of what he really wills here. Does he want wealth? What anxiety, envy, and traps might he bring upon himself? Does he want knowledge and insight? These may merely sharpen his vision, revealing more terribly the unavoidable evils now hidden from him, or burden his desires with still more needs, though they already trouble him enough. Does he want a long life? Who guarantees it will not be a long misery? Health, at least? How often bodily discomfort restrains us from excesses into which perfect health would let us fall. And so on. In short, no principle lets him determine with certainty what would make him truly happy: that would require omniscience. To secure happiness, we can therefore follow only empirical counsels, not definite principles: advice about regimen, frugality, courtesy, reserve, and so forth, which experience shows usually best promote well-being. Strictly speaking, then, imperatives of prudence do not command at all. They cannot present actions as objectively, practically necessary and should be considered counsels, consilia, rather than rational precepts. The problem of determining certainly and universally which action would promote a rational being’s happiness is entirely insoluble. No imperative can therefore strictly command us to do what makes us happy. Happiness is an ideal of imagination, not reason, resting solely on empirical grounds. We cannot expect those grounds to specify an action securing the totality of a series of consequences that is actually endless. Yet if we assume the means to happiness could be determined with certainty, the imperative of prudence would be analytical. Its only difference from an imperative of skill is that here the end is given, whereas there it is merely possible. Both prescribe only means to something assumed to be willed as an end. In both cases, therefore, the imperative directing whoever wills the end to will the means is analytical. The possibility of this kind of imperative presents no difficulty either.

By contrast, the question of how the imperative of morality is possible unquestionably demands an answer and a solution; indeed, this is the only kind of imperative for which that is needed. It is not hypothetical at all, and its objective necessity cannot depend on a hypothesis as hypothetical imperatives do. We must always remember, however, that no example—nothing empirical—can establish whether such an imperative exists at all. We must rather fear that imperatives appearing categorical may ultimately be hypothetical. Take the precept "Thou shalt not promise deceitfully". Suppose its necessity is not merely advice to avoid another evil, meaning "Thou shalt not make a lying promise, lest if it become known thou shouldst destroy thy credit," but instead treats such an action as evil in itself, making the prohibition categorical. Even then, no example can show with certainty that the law alone determined the will, without any other motive, however much this seems to be the case. Fear of disgrace, perhaps also a dim dread of other dangers, may always be secretly influencing the will. How can experience prove a cause nonexistent when it tells us only that we do not perceive it? In that case, the supposedly moral imperative, appearing categorical and unconditional, would really be a pragmatic precept, directing attention to our own interests and teaching us merely to consider them.

We must therefore investigate, entirely a priori, how it is possible for there to be a categorical imperative. Here we do not have its actuality given in experience, so that explaining its possibility would merely elucidate it rather than establish it. Meanwhile, we can already see that only the categorical imperative has the force of a practical law. The others may be called principles of the will, but not laws: whatever is necessary only for an arbitrary purpose is contingent in itself, and we can always escape the precept by abandoning the purpose. An unconditional command, however, gives the will no freedom to choose the opposite. It alone therefore carries the necessity required of a law.

Second, understanding the possibility of this categorical imperative, or law of morality, presents a very deep difficulty. It is an a priori synthetical practical proposition. * Since establishing the possibility of speculative propositions of this kind is so difficult, we can readily expect practical ones to be no less difficult.

* I connect the action with the will a priori, without presupposing any condition arising from inclination, and therefore necessarily. This necessity is only objective: it assumes a reason with complete power over all subjective motives. The resulting practical proposition does not analytically derive the willing of an action from another act of willing already presupposed, for we do not possess such a perfect will. Rather, it directly joins the action’s willing to the concept of a rational being’s will, as something not contained in that concept.

In tackling this problem, we shall first ask whether the bare concept of a categorical imperative might also yield its formula, containing the proposition that alone can be such an imperative. Even once we know what this absolute command says, explaining how it is possible will require further, separate, painstaking inquiry, which we shall reserve for the final section.

When I conceive a hypothetical imperative, I generally cannot know its content in advance until its condition is supplied. Conceiving a categorical imperative, however, immediately tells me its content. Besides the law, the imperative contains only the necessity that maxims * conform to it, while the law contains no restrictive conditions. What remains is simply the general requirement that the action’s maxim conform to a universal law. That conformity alone is what the imperative properly presents as necessary.

* A maxim is a subjective principle of action, distinct from the objective principle, the practical law. It contains a practical rule laid down by reason according to the subject’s conditions, often its ignorance or inclinations, and is thus the principle on which the subject acts. The law, however, is the objective principle valid for every rational being: the principle on which it ought to act, that is, an imperative.
There is therefore just one categorical imperative: act only on a maxim that you can at the same time will to become a universal law.

If every imperative of duty can be derived from this single imperative as its principle, we shall at least be able to explain what we understand by duty and what the concept means, even if it remains undecided whether duty is anything more than an empty concept.

Nature, in its most general, formal sense, consists in the universality of the law according to which effects occur: the existence of things insofar as general laws determine it. We can therefore express the imperative of duty this way: act as though, through your will, your action’s maxim were to become a universal law of nature.
Let us now list a few duties, using the customary division into duties to ourselves and to others, and into perfect and imperfect duties. *

* I shall reserve the division of duties for a future metaphysics of morals, so the division given here is merely an arbitrary arrangement of my examples. By a perfect duty I mean one permitting no exception for inclination. I therefore recognise internal as well as external perfect duties. This differs from the schools’ use of the term, but I shall not defend it here: whether it is accepted makes no difference to my present purpose.

1. A man driven to despair by repeated misfortunes is tired of life, yet retains enough reason to ask whether taking his life would violate his duty to himself. He asks whether his action’s maxim could become a universal law of nature. His maxim is: "From self-love I adopt it as a principle to shorten my life when its longer duration is likely to bring more evil than satisfaction." The question is simply whether this principle, based on self-love, can become a universal law of nature. We immediately see that a natural system would contradict itself if its law destroyed life through the very feeling whose distinctive function is to encourage life’s improvement. Such a system of nature could not exist. This maxim therefore cannot possibly exist as a universal law of nature and is wholly incompatible with the supreme principle of every duty.

2. Another man finds himself compelled by necessity to borrow money. He knows he cannot repay it, but also knows no one will lend unless he firmly promises repayment by a particular date. He wants to make the promise, yet has enough conscience to ask: "Is it not unlawful and inconsistent with duty to get out of a difficulty in this way?" Suppose he nevertheless decides to proceed. His maxim would be: "When I think myself in want of money, I will borrow money and promise to repay it, although I know that I never can do so." This principle of self-love or personal advantage might agree with my entire future welfare, but the present question is, "Is it right?" I therefore turn self-love’s suggestion into a universal law and ask: "How would it be if my maxim were a universal law?" I immediately see it could never hold as a universal law of nature, because it would necessarily contradict itself. Suppose everyone in difficulty could promise whatever he liked without intending to keep it. The promise itself, and any end sought through it, would become impossible. No one would believe anything had been promised; everyone would laugh at such statements as empty pretences.

3. A third man discovers a talent in himself that cultivation could make useful in many ways. But he lives comfortably and would rather enjoy himself than work to expand and improve his fortunate natural abilities. Still, he asks whether neglecting those gifts agrees with duty as well as with his inclination to pleasure. He sees that a system of nature could indeed exist under such a universal law, even if people, like the South Sea islanders, left their talents idle and devoted life solely to idleness, amusement, and reproducing their species—in a word, enjoyment. Yet he cannot possibly will this as a universal law of nature or as a natural instinct implanted in us. As a rational being, he necessarily wills the development of his faculties, since they serve him, and were given to him, for every sort of possible purpose.

4. A fourth man enjoys prosperity and sees others struggling with great misery, although he could help them. He thinks: "What concern is it of mine? Let everyone be as happy as Heaven pleases, or as he can make himself; I will take nothing from him nor even envy him, only I do not wish to contribute anything to his welfare or to his assistance in distress!" Humanity could undoubtedly survive if this attitude became a universal law. It might even fare better than where everyone speaks of sympathy and goodwill, occasionally practises them, yet also cheats whenever possible, betrays people’s rights, or otherwise violates them. A universal law of nature conforming to this maxim is therefore possible. But willing such a principle to have the universal force of a natural law is impossible. That will would contradict itself: many situations might arise in which the man needed others’ love and sympathy, yet a law of nature originating in his own will would deprive him of every hope of the help he desired.

These are only a few among many actual duties, or at least what we regard as duties. They plainly fall into two classes under our single principle. We must be able to will our action’s maxim as a universal law: this is the general standard for morally evaluating an action. Some actions have maxims that cannot even be conceived without contradiction as universal laws of nature, much less willed as such. Other maxims involve no such intrinsic impossibility, yet cannot be willed as universal laws of nature, since such a will would contradict itself. The first sort clearly violates strict, rigorous, inflexible duty; the second violates only wider, meritorious duty. We have thus fully shown how all duties, with regard to the nature of their obligation rather than their actions’ objects, depend on the same principle.

When we examine ourselves in a breach of duty, we find that we do not actually will our maxim as a universal law: that is impossible for us. We want the opposite maxim to remain a universal law, while taking the liberty of an exception for ourselves or, just this once, for our inclination. If we considered every case from reason’s single standpoint, we would find our will contradicting itself. It would require a principle to be objectively necessary as a universal law, yet subjectively not universal, permitting exceptions. But we shift between viewpoints at different moments: first we regard our action from the standpoint of a will wholly conforming to reason, then we regard that very same action from the standpoint of a will influenced by inclination. There is therefore not really a contradiction, but a conflict between inclination and reason’s command. This changes the principle’s universality into mere generality, making reason’s practical principle meet the maxim halfway. Although our own impartial judgement cannot justify this, it proves that we do recognise the categorical imperative’s validity. With all respect for it, we merely allow ourselves a few exceptions that we consider unimportant and forced upon us.
