We have now established at least this much: that, if duty is to have meaning and genuine legislative authority over our actions, it must be expressed through categorical imperatives, never hypothetical ones. We have also clearly and definitely presented the categorical imperative’s content for every practical application, an important result. If duty exists at all, this imperative must contain its principle. But we have not yet proved a priori that such an imperative actually exists: that a practical law commands absolutely, of itself and without any further motive, and that obeying this law is duty.

To reach that proof, it is essential to remember that we must not even consider deriving this principle’s actuality from the special attributes of human nature. Duty must be an unconditional practical necessity of action. It must therefore apply to every rational being to which an imperative can apply at all, and only for that reason be a law for every human will as well. Anything derived from humanity’s particular natural characteristics—from certain feelings and tendencies, or even, if possible, from a tendency peculiar to human reason that need not hold for every rational being’s will—can provide a maxim, but never a law. It supplies a subjective principle we may feel disposed or inclined to follow, not an objective principle commanding us to act even if every tendency, inclination, and natural disposition opposes it. Indeed, the fewer subjective impulses favour duty’s command, and the more they resist it, the more clearly its sublimity and intrinsic dignity appear. Those impulses cannot in the slightest weaken the law’s obligation or diminish its validity.

Philosophy now faces a critical situation: it must hold its ground firmly, although nothing in heaven or on earth supports it. Here it must display its purity as the absolute director of its own laws, not as the messenger of laws whispered by some implanted sense or unknown guardian nature. Such whispers may be better than nothing, but they can never supply principles dictated by reason. Those principles must originate wholly a priori and derive their commanding authority from that origin. They expect everything from the law’s supremacy and the respect owed to it, nothing from inclination; otherwise, they condemn the person to self-contempt and inward abhorrence.

Every empirical element is therefore not merely incapable of supporting morality’s principle; it seriously damages morality’s purity. The distinctive, priceless worth of an absolutely good will lies precisely in its principle of action being free from all influence of contingent grounds, the only grounds experience can supply. We cannot warn too strongly or too often against this lax, even base way of thinking that searches among empirical motives and laws for its principle. Weary human reason gladly rests on this pillow. Dreaming sweet illusions—in which it embraces a cloud instead of Juno—it replaces morality with a bastard patched together from limbs of different origins. The result looks like anything one wishes to see in it, except virtue, to anyone who has once seen her true form. *

* Seeing virtue in her proper form means contemplating morality stripped of every admixture of sensible things and every false ornament of reward or self-love. With the slightest exercise of reason, anyone whose capacity for abstraction is not entirely spoiled can readily see how completely she then eclipses everything else that attracts our feelings.

The question is therefore: "Is it a necessary law for all rational beings that they should always judge of their actions by maxims of which they can themselves will that they should serve as universal laws?" If so, this law must be connected wholly a priori with the very concept of a rational being’s will in general. To discover that connection, however reluctantly, we must enter metaphysics—not speculative philosophy, but its distinct domain of the metaphysics of morals. Practical philosophy seeks laws of what ought to happen, even if it never happens, rather than causes of what does happen: it seeks objective practical laws. It therefore need not ask why something pleases or displeases, how sensory pleasure differs from taste, whether taste differs from reason’s general satisfaction, what underlies feelings of pleasure and pain, or how these produce desires and inclinations that, with reason’s cooperation, yield maxims. All this belongs to empirical psychology, which would constitute the second part of physics if physics means the philosophy of nature insofar as it rests on empirical laws. Here, however, we concern ourselves with objective practical laws and thus with the will’s relation to itself insofar as reason alone determines it. Everything referring to the empirical is necessarily excluded. If reason alone determines conduct—and its ability to do so is what we are investigating—it must necessarily determine it a priori.

We conceive the will as the faculty of determining oneself to act according to the conception of certain laws. Only rational beings can possess this faculty. What serves as the objective ground of the will’s self-determination is called the end; if reason alone supplies it, it must hold for every rational being. What merely grounds the possibility of an action whose effect is the end is called the means. The subjective ground of desire is the spring; the objective ground of willing is the motive. We thus distinguish subjective ends based on springs from objective ends based on motives valid for every rational being. Practical principles are formal when they abstract from all subjective ends, material when they presuppose such ends and therefore particular springs of action. Ends a rational being freely chooses as effects of his actions—material ends—are all relative. Their worth comes solely from their relation to the subject’s particular desires. Such worth cannot supply principles universally necessary for every rational being and every act of willing, that is, practical laws. These relative ends can therefore yield only hypothetical imperatives.

Suppose, however, something existed whose existence possessed absolute worth in itself: something that, as an end in itself, could provide a source of definite laws. In that alone would lie the source of a possible categorical imperative, or practical law.

Now I maintain that a human being, and generally every rational being, exists as an end in himself, not merely as a means available for arbitrary use by one will or another. In every action, whether concerning himself or other rational beings, he must always be regarded at the same time as an end. Objects of inclination have only conditional worth: without the inclinations and the needs arising from them, their objects would have no value. But inclinations themselves generate need. Far from possessing absolute worth that would make them desirable, they are something every rational being must universally wish to be wholly free of. Thus any object acquired through our action always has conditional worth. Beings whose existence depends on nature’s will rather than ours, if non-rational, still possess only relative value as means and are called things. Rational beings, however, are called persons because their nature marks them as ends in themselves: as something never to be used merely as a means, thereby limiting freedom of action and commanding respect. They are not merely subjective ends, whose existence has value for us as an effect of our action, but objective ends: beings whose existence is itself an end. No other end can replace them and reduce them to mere means. Otherwise nothing would possess absolute worth; and if every worth were conditional and therefore contingent, reason would have no supreme practical principle at all.

If there is a supreme practical principle—or, in relation to the human will, a categorical imperative—it must derive from the concept of what is necessarily an end for everyone because it is an end in itself. It must constitute an objective principle of the will and so serve as a universal practical law. Its foundation is this: rational nature exists as an end in itself. A human being necessarily conceives his own existence this way; to that extent it is a subjective principle of human action. But every other rational being regards its existence in the same way, on precisely the rational principle that applies to me. * It is therefore also an objective principle, from which every law of the will must be derivable as from a supreme practical law. The practical imperative is accordingly: act so that you always treat humanity, in your own person or anyone else’s, at the same time as an end, never merely as a means. We shall now ask whether this can be put into practice.
* I state this proposition here as a postulate. Its grounding will be supplied in the concluding section.
Let us stay with our earlier examples:

First, consider necessary duty to oneself. Someone contemplating suicide should ask whether his action agrees with humanity as an end in itself. Destroying himself to escape painful circumstances would use a person merely as a means of maintaining a tolerable condition until life’s end. But a human being is not a thing, something usable merely as a means. In every action he must always also be regarded as an end in himself. I therefore cannot dispose of the human being in my own person by mutilating, harming, or killing him. (Ethics proper must define this principle more precisely to prevent misunderstandings: for example, about amputating limbs to preserve my life, risking my life in order to save it, and similar cases. I therefore leave that question aside here.)

Second, consider necessary duties towards others, those of strict obligation. Someone thinking of making a false promise to other people will immediately see that he would be using another person merely as a means, without that person also containing the end in himself. The person I propose to use for my own purposes through the promise cannot possibly agree to my way of treating him, and therefore cannot himself contain this action’s end. This violation of humanity’s principle in others is still clearer in attacks on their freedom or property. Someone who violates human rights plainly intends to use others merely as means, failing to consider that, as rational beings, they must always also be valued as ends: as beings capable of containing within themselves the end of that very action. *

* Do not suppose that the familiar "quod tibi non vis fieri, etc." can serve as our rule or principle. It is merely a deduction from the preceding principle, subject to several restrictions, and cannot be a universal law. It includes neither duties to oneself nor duties of benevolence towards others: many people would gladly forgo others’ help if excused from helping them. Nor does it include duties of strict obligation to one another, since a criminal could use this principle to argue against the judge punishing him, and so forth.

Third, consider contingent, meritorious duties to oneself. Merely avoiding violations of humanity in our own person as an end in itself is insufficient; our actions must also harmonise with it. Humanity contains capacities for greater perfection, belonging to nature’s purpose for humanity in us as its subject. Neglecting them might be compatible with preserving humanity as an end in itself, but not with advancing that end.

Fourth, consider meritorious duties towards others. Everyone naturally seeks his own happiness. Humanity could indeed survive if no one contributed to another’s happiness, provided no one deliberately diminished it. Yet this would agree only negatively, not positively, with humanity as an end in itself, unless everyone also did what he could to advance others’ ends. If the concept is to have its full effect on me, the ends of a subject who is an end in himself must, as far as possible, also become my ends.

The principle that humanity, and every rational nature generally, is an end in itself—the supreme limit on everyone’s freedom of action—is not taken from experience. First, it applies universally to all rational beings whatsoever, about whom experience can establish nothing. Second, it does not present humanity as an end for human beings subjectively, as an object they actually choose as an end. It presents humanity as an objective end that, as a law, must set the supreme limit to all our subjective ends, whatever they may be. It must therefore arise from pure reason. According to our first principle, the objective basis of all practical legislation lies in the rule and its universal form, which enables it to be a law, for example a law of nature. The subjective basis, however, lies in the end. According to the second principle, every rational being is the subject of all ends insofar as it is an end in itself. From this follows a third practical principle of the will, the ultimate condition of its agreement with universal practical reason: the idea of every rational being’s will as a universally legislative will.

This principle rejects every maxim incompatible with the will’s own role as universal legislator. The will is thus subject to the law in a particular way: it must be regarded as itself giving that law and, only on that basis, as subject to a law whose author it can consider itself to be.

Our earlier imperatives rested, respectively, on actions’ conformity to general laws as in a physical system of nature, and on rational beings’ universal prerogative as ends in themselves. Precisely because we conceived them as categorical, we excluded any interest as a spring of action from sharing in their authority. Yet we only assumed they were categorical because that assumption was necessary to explain duty’s concept. We could not independently prove that practical propositions commanding categorically actually exist, nor can that be proved in this section. We could, however, use a definite expression within the imperative itself to indicate that willing from duty renounces every interest. This is the distinctive criterion separating categorical from hypothetical imperatives. Our present, third formula does precisely that, through the idea of every rational being’s will as a will that legislates universally.

A will subject to laws may indeed be bound to a law through an interest. But a will that is itself the supreme lawgiver cannot, insofar as it is such, depend on any interest. A will that depended on interest would still require another law limiting its self-love by the condition of validity as universal law.

Thus the principle that every human will is a will that gives universal laws through every one of its maxims, * if otherwise justified, would be particularly suited to serve as the categorical imperative. The idea of universal legislation makes it independent of interest, and therefore the only possible unconditional imperative. Better still, reversing the proposition: if a categorical imperative exists—a law for every rational being’s will—it can only command that everything be done according to maxims of a will that could simultaneously will itself to give universal laws. Only then are the practical principle and the imperative it follows unconditional, because neither can rest on any interest.
* I may be excused from adding examples to clarify this principle: every example already used to explain the categorical imperative and its formula would serve equally well here.

Looking back at earlier attempts to discover morality’s principle, we need not wonder why all failed. They recognised that duty bound human beings to laws, but overlooked that the laws binding them must be their own, while also being universal. A person is bound only to act in accordance with his own will—a will, however, naturally fitted to give universal laws. Once a person is conceived merely as subject to some law, whatever it is, that law requires an interest to attract or constrain him. It does not originate as law in his own will; instead, something else obliges his will, under a law, to act in a certain way. This inevitable consequence rendered all the effort to find duty’s supreme principle irretrievably wasted. What emerged was never duty, only the necessity of acting from an interest. Whether private or otherwise, that interest necessarily made the imperative conditional, incapable of being a moral command. I shall therefore call our principle the autonomy of the will, in contrast with every other principle, which I accordingly classify as heteronomy.

The concept of every rational being’s will as a will that must regard itself as giving universal laws through all its maxims, and judge both itself and its actions from that standpoint, leads to a further concept dependent on it and highly fruitful: a kingdom of ends.

By a kingdom I mean a systematic union of different rational beings under common laws. Laws determine the universal validity of ends. If we therefore abstract from rational beings’ personal differences and from the entire content of their private ends, we can conceive all ends united into one systematic whole. This includes rational beings as ends in themselves and the particular ends each may choose. In other words, we can conceive a kingdom of ends, made possible by the principles already established.

Every rational being is subject to the law that it must treat itself and all others never merely as means, but always simultaneously as ends in themselves. This produces a systematic union of rational beings through shared objective laws: a kingdom. Since those laws concern precisely these beings’ relations to one another as ends and means, we may call it a kingdom of ends. It is, to be sure, only an ideal.

A rational being is a member of the kingdom of ends when it gives universal laws within that kingdom while also being subject to them. It is sovereign when it gives laws without being subject to anyone else’s will.

A rational being must always regard itself as a legislator, either member or sovereign, in a kingdom of ends made possible by freedom of the will. But its will’s maxims alone cannot establish sovereignty. That requires a completely independent being, without needs and possessing unrestricted power adequate to its will.

Morality therefore consists in relating every action to the legislation that alone makes a kingdom of ends possible. This legislation must be capable of existing in every rational being and proceeding from its will. The will’s principle is consequently never to act on a maxim that cannot also, without contradiction, be a universal law: always to act so that the will can simultaneously regard itself as giving universal laws through its maxims. When rational beings’ maxims do not naturally agree with this objective principle, the necessity of acting on it is called practical necessitation, or duty. Duty does not apply to the kingdom of ends’ sovereign. It applies to every member, and to all in equal measure.

The practical necessity of acting on this principle—duty—rests neither on feelings, impulses, nor inclinations, but entirely on rational beings’ relations to one another. In these relations a rational being’s will must always be regarded as legislative; otherwise the being could not be conceived as an end in itself. Reason therefore relates each maxim of a universally legislating will to every other will and to every action towards oneself. It does so without any further practical motive or prospective advantage, solely through the idea of a rational being’s dignity: obeying no law except one that it also gives itself.

In the kingdom of ends, everything possesses either value or dignity. Something with value can be exchanged for an equivalent. Something above all value, admitting no equivalent at all, possesses dignity instead.

What relates to humanity’s general inclinations and needs has a market value. What satisfies a particular taste without presupposing a need—pleasure in our faculties’ mere purposeless play—has a fancy value. But what constitutes the condition under which alone something can be an end in itself has more than relative worth, or value. It has intrinsic worth: dignity.

Morality alone makes it possible for a rational being to be an end in himself, because only through morality can he be a legislating member of the kingdom of ends. Morality, and humanity insofar as it is capable of morality, therefore alone possess dignity. Skill and diligence at work have market value; wit, vivid imagination, and humour have fancy value. Keeping promises and acting benevolently from principle rather than instinct, by contrast, have intrinsic worth. Neither nature nor art can supply substitutes if these are lacking. Their worth does not lie in their effects or the uses and advantages they secure, but in the disposition of mind: the will’s maxims, ready to express themselves in these actions even when the intended effects fail to follow. Nor do these actions need subjective taste or sentiment to recommend them to our immediate favour and satisfaction. They require no immediate attraction or feeling. They present the will performing them as an object of direct respect. Reason alone is needed to impose them on the will, not to coax it into them, which would contradict the nature of duty. This assessment shows that such a disposition possesses dignity, placing it infinitely above all value. We cannot compare it or set it in competition with value even for a moment without, as it were, violating its sanctity.

What entitles virtue, the morally good disposition, to make such exalted claims? Nothing less than the privilege it grants a rational being of participating in universal legislation, thereby qualifying him for membership in a possible kingdom of ends. His own nature already destined him for this privilege: as an end in himself, he legislates in that kingdom, free in relation to all physical laws of nature, obeying only laws he gives himself. Through these laws his maxims can belong to a system of universal law to which he also submits. Nothing has worth beyond what the law assigns it. The legislation that assigns worth to everything must therefore itself possess dignity: unconditional, incomparable worth. Only the word respect adequately expresses the esteem a rational being must have for it. Autonomy is thus the basis of the dignity of human nature and of every rational nature.

Our three ways of presenting morality’s principle are fundamentally three formulas of exactly the same law, each containing the other two. They do differ, but in a subjectively rather than objectively practical way. Through a certain kind of analogy, they aim to bring an idea of reason closer to intuition and therefore to feeling. Every maxim, in fact, has:
1. A form, consisting in universality. From this perspective the moral imperative’s formula says that maxims must be chosen as though they were to serve as universal laws of nature.

2. A matter, namely an end. Here the formula says that the rational being, an end by its own nature and therefore an end in itself, must in every maxim limit all ends that are merely relative and arbitrary.

3. A complete characterisation of all maxims through the formula that their own legislation must make them agree with a possible kingdom of ends as with a kingdom of nature. * This progression follows the categories: unity of the will’s form, its universality; plurality of its matter, the objects or ends; and totality of their system. When judging actions morally, it is better always to follow the strict method, beginning with the categorical imperative’s general formula: act on a maxim that can simultaneously make itself a universal law. If we want the moral law to gain admission, however, it is very useful to consider one and the same action under all three concepts, bringing it as close to intuition as possible.

* Teleology views nature as a kingdom of ends; ethics views a possible kingdom of ends as a kingdom of nature. In the first, the kingdom of ends is a theoretical idea used to explain what actually exists. In the second, it is a practical idea used to produce what does not yet exist but can be realised through our conduct, if that conduct conforms to the idea.

We can now finish where we began, with the concept of an unconditionally good will. An absolutely good will cannot be evil: its maxim, made a universal law, could never contradict itself. Its supreme law is therefore: "Act always on such a maxim as thou canst at the same time will to be a universal law". This is the only condition under which a will can never contradict itself, and this imperative is categorical. The will’s validity as a universal law for possible actions resembles the universal connection of existing things through general laws—the formal concept of nature in general. We can therefore also state the categorical imperative as follows: act on maxims that can simultaneously take themselves as universal laws of nature for their object. This, then, is the formula of an absolutely good will.

Rational nature differs from the rest of nature by setting itself an end. That end would supply every good will’s matter. But the idea of a will absolutely good, unlimited by any condition of achieving this or that end, requires complete abstraction from every end to be produced, since such an end would make the will only relatively good. Here, therefore, we must conceive the end as independently existing, not as something to be brought about. It is conceived negatively: as something against which we must never act, never regard merely as a means, and must always also esteem as an end in every act of willing. This end can only be the subject of all possible ends, which is also the subject of a possible absolutely good will; subordinating such a will to any other object would contradict it. The principle "So act in regard to every rational being (thyself and others), that he may always have place in thy maxim as an end in himself," is thus essentially identical with "Act upon a maxim which, at the same time, involves its own universal validity for every rational being." Limiting my maxim in every use of means by requiring it to hold as law for every subject amounts to the same thing as making this the fundamental principle of all maxims: the subject of all ends, the rational being himself, must never be used merely as a means. He must instead be the supreme condition limiting every use of means, and therefore always also an end.

It follows beyond dispute that a rational being, whatever laws bind him, must as an end in himself be able to regard himself as universally legislating those same laws. The fitness of his maxims for universal legislation is precisely what distinguishes him as an end in himself. This also constitutes his dignity, his prerogative above merely physical beings. He must always adopt maxims from the standpoint that regards both himself and every other rational being as legislators, and hence as persons. Through legislation belonging to all persons as members, a world of rational beings, mundus intelligibilis, thus becomes possible as a kingdom of ends. Every rational being must therefore act as though his maxims always made him a legislating member of that universal kingdom. Their formal principle is: "So act as if thy maxim were to serve likewise as the universal law (of all rational beings)." A kingdom of ends is possible only by analogy with a kingdom of nature. The former operates through maxims, self-imposed rules; the latter through laws of efficient causes necessitated from outside. Although nature’s system is seen as a machine, its reference to rational beings as ends nevertheless earns it the name kingdom of nature. A kingdom of ends would actually be realised if everyone followed maxims conforming to the standard the categorical imperative prescribes to all rational beings. Yet a rational being who follows this maxim exactly cannot count on everyone else doing likewise. Nor can he expect nature’s kingdom and orderly arrangements to harmonise with him as a fitting member of the kingdom of ends he helps constitute—in other words, to favour his expectation of happiness. Nonetheless, the law "Act according to the maxims of a member of a merely possible kingdom of ends legislating in it universally," retains full authority because it commands categorically. Here lies the paradox: human dignity as a rational creature, without any further end or advantage—respect for a mere idea—must nevertheless serve as an inflexible command to the will. The maxim’s independence of every such spring of action is precisely its sublimity. This makes every rational subject worthy of legislative membership in the kingdom of ends; otherwise he could only be conceived as subject to the physical law of his needs. Suppose, moreover, the kingdom of nature and kingdom of ends were united under one sovereign, so that the latter ceased to be merely an idea and became actual. It would certainly gain a powerful spring of action, but no additional intrinsic worth. Even then, this sole absolute legislator must be conceived as assessing rational beings’ worth only through their disinterested conduct, prescribed to themselves solely from that idea [the dignity of man]. External relations do not alter things’ essence. What alone constitutes humanity’s absolute worth, apart from those relations, must also be the standard of judgement whoever judges, even the Supreme Being. Morality is therefore the relation of actions to the will’s autonomy, to potential universal legislation through its maxims. Actions consistent with autonomy of the will are permitted; those inconsistent with it are forbidden. A will whose maxims necessarily agree with autonomy’s laws is holy, absolutely good. Obligation is a will that is not absolutely good depending on autonomy’s principle—moral necessitation. Obligation cannot apply to a holy being. The objective necessity of actions arising from obligation is called duty.

From what has just been said, we can now readily understand why we attribute dignity and sublimity to someone who fulfils every duty, although duty implies subjection to law. Mere subjection to the moral law gives him no sublimity. He has it because he also legislates that very law and is subject to it only on that account. We have likewise shown that respect for the law alone, rather than fear or inclination, is the spring capable of giving actions moral worth. The proper object of respect is our own will, conceived as acting only on the condition that its maxims could be universal laws: the ideal will possible for us. Humanity’s dignity lies precisely in this capacity for universal legislation, subject to the condition that it remains bound by that same legislation.
The Autonomy of the Will as the Supreme Principle of Morality

Autonomy is the will’s property of being a law to itself, independently of any property of the objects it wills. The principle of autonomy is therefore: "Always so to choose that the same volition shall comprehend the maxims of our choice as a universal law." Merely analysing the concepts within this practical rule cannot prove that it is an imperative, a condition necessarily binding every rational being’s will. It is a synthetical proposition. We must move beyond knowledge of the objects to critically examine the subject, pure practical reason. This synthetic proposition commands apodeictically and must therefore be knowable entirely a priori. That inquiry does not belong in this section. Mere analysis of moral concepts can, however, readily show that this principle of autonomy is morality’s only principle. Such analysis reveals that morality’s principle must be a categorical imperative, which commands neither more nor less than precisely this autonomy.
Heteronomy of the Will as the Source of all spurious Principles
of Morality

If the will seeks its determining law anywhere except in its maxims’ fitness to be universal laws of its own making—if it leaves itself and looks for that law in some object’s character—the result is always heteronomy. The will then receives the law from the object through the object’s relation to it, rather than giving itself the law. Whether based on inclination or rational concepts, this relation permits only hypothetical imperatives: "I ought to do something because I wish for something else." The moral, categorical imperative instead says: "I ought to do so and so, even though I should not wish for anything else." For example, the former says: "I ought not to lie, if I would retain my reputation"; the latter says: "I ought not to lie, although it should not bring me the least discredit." The latter must abstract from all objects sufficiently to prevent their influencing the will. Practical reason, the will, must not be confined to administering an interest foreign to itself, but must display its own commanding authority as supreme legislation. Thus I ought to promote others’ happiness, not because its realisation concerns me through immediate inclination or through satisfaction indirectly mediated by reason, but simply because a maxim excluding it cannot be included as universal law in one and the same act of willing.
Classification of all Principles of Morality which can be
founded on the Conception of Heteronomy
Here, as elsewhere, human reason in its pure use, before being critically examined, first tried every possible wrong path before finally finding the single true one.

Principles adopted from this standpoint are either empirical or rational. Empirical principles derive from happiness and rest on physical or moral feelings. Rational principles derive from perfection and rest either on the rational concept of perfection as a possible effect or on independent perfection, the will of God, as the cause determining our will.

Empirical principles cannot possibly ground moral laws. Moral laws must apply universally to all rational beings without distinction and impose unconditional practical necessity on them. Both features disappear if the laws are based on humanity’s particular constitution or the accidental circumstances surrounding it. The principle of private happiness is the most objectionable. This is not merely because it is false, with experience contradicting the claim that prosperity always corresponds to good conduct. Nor is it merely because it does nothing to establish morality: making someone prosperous is quite different from making him good, and making him prudent and perceptive about his interests differs from making him virtuous. Rather, the springs it offers morality undermine morality and destroy its sublimity. They place motives to virtue and vice in a single class, teaching only better calculation and erasing the specific difference between them. Appealing to moral feeling, a supposed special sense, * is likewise superficial: those unable to think imagine feeling will rescue them, even in matters of universal laws. Feelings naturally vary enormously in degree and cannot furnish a uniform standard of good and evil; no one is entitled to judge for others by his own feelings. Nevertheless, moral feeling comes closer to morality and its dignity in one respect: it honours virtue by attributing our satisfaction and esteem directly to her, instead of, so to speak, telling her to her face that profit, not her beauty, attracts us.

* I place moral feeling under happiness because every empirical interest promises to improve our well-being through something’s agreeableness, whether immediately and without thought of profit, or with profit in view. We must likewise follow Hutcheson in placing sympathy with others’ happiness under the moral sense he assumes.

Among rational moral principles, the ontological concept of perfection, despite its defects, is preferable to the theological concept deriving morality from an absolutely perfect Divine will. The former is admittedly empty and indefinite, and therefore useless for discovering the greatest amount of reality appropriate to us within the boundless field of possible reality. Moreover, in trying to distinguish the particular reality at issue from every other kind, it inevitably circles back and tacitly presupposes the morality it is meant to explain. It is nevertheless preferable to theology for two reasons. First, we have no intuition of divine perfection and can derive it only from our own concepts, foremost among them morality; our explanation would therefore become blatantly circular. Second, if we avoid that circle, the only concept of the Divine will left is assembled from desires for glory and dominion together with terrifying ideas of power and vengeance. Any moral system founded on that would directly oppose morality.

If, however, I had to make a choice between moral sense and perfection in general—two systems that at least do not weaken morality, though neither can possibly ground it—I would choose the latter. It at least removes the decision from sensibility and brings it before pure reason’s court. Although it settles nothing even there, it preserves the indefinite idea of a will good in itself, uncorrupted, until that idea receives a more precise definition.

I think I can be excused from refuting all these doctrines in detail here. That would be unnecessary work: the refutation is easy and probably evident even to those whose office requires them to endorse one theory because their audiences would not tolerate suspended judgement. What matters more for us is that every one of these principles makes heteronomy of the will morality’s primary foundation. For that reason, they must necessarily fail in their aim.

Whenever prescribing the rule determining the will requires us to presuppose an object of the will, the rule is simply heteronomy. The imperative is conditional: if, or because, one wants this object, one should act in this way. It can therefore never command morally, or categorically. The object may determine the will through inclination, as with private happiness, or through reason directed towards objects of possible willing generally, as with perfection. In either case the will never determines itself directly through the concept of the action. Instead, the anticipated effect influences the will: I ought to do something because I want something else. This presupposes another law within me as subject, under which I necessarily will that other thing; and that law again needs an imperative restricting the maxim. An object within our powers can, through its natural properties, influence the subject’s will only in a way dependent on the subject’s nature. This may be sensibility, inclination and taste, or understanding and reason, whose exercise brings satisfaction because of their particular natural constitution. The law would therefore, properly speaking, be given by nature. It would have to be known and established through experience, making it contingent and incapable of being an apodeictic practical rule, as a moral rule must be. Moreover, it remains inevitably heteronomy: a foreign impulse supplies the law through a receptive natural constitution of the subject, instead of the will legislating for itself. An absolutely good will, whose principle must be a categorical imperative, is therefore indeterminate with respect to every object and contains only the form of willing in general, as autonomy. That is, the capacity of every good will’s maxims to make themselves a universal law is itself the sole law every rational being’s will imposes on itself, without needing to presuppose any spring or interest as its foundation.

How such a synthetical practical a priori proposition is possible, and why it is necessary, cannot be resolved within the metaphysics of morals. We have not affirmed its truth here, much less claimed to possess a proof. We have only unfolded the universally accepted concept of morality to show that autonomy of the will is inseparably connected with it—or, rather, grounds it. Anyone who regards morality as real, not a fantasy without truth, must therefore also accept the principle assigned to it here. This section, like the first, has been purely analytical. To prove that morality is no invention of the mind—which it cannot be if the categorical imperative and the will’s autonomy are true and absolutely necessary as an a priori principle—requires the possibility of a synthetic use of pure practical reason. We cannot venture upon this without first critically examining that faculty of reason. The final section will outline the main features of this critical examination as far as our purpose requires.

chapters.title: Section III — Transition from the Metaphysics of Morals to the Critique of Pure Practical Reason
paragraphs: The Concept of Freedom is the Key to Explaining the Autonomy of the Will

The will is a kind of causality belonging to living beings insofar as they are rational. Freedom would be the property enabling this causality to act independently of external causes determining it. Physical necessity, by contrast, is the property of non-rational beings’ causality by which external causes determine it to act.
This definition of freedom is negative and therefore cannot fruitfully disclose freedom’s essence. It does, however, lead to a positive concept that is all the richer and more fruitful.

Causality involves laws by which something we call a cause must produce something else, its effect. Thus, although freedom is not a property of the will dependent on physical laws, it is not lawless. It must instead be a causality operating under unchanging laws of a special kind; otherwise a free will would be absurd. Physical necessity is the heteronomy of efficient causes. Every effect is possible only under the law that something else determines the efficient cause to exercise its causality. What, then, could freedom of the will be except autonomy, the will’s property of being its own law? The proposition "The will is in every action a law to itself," simply expresses the principle "To act on no other maxim than that which can also have as an object itself as a universal law." This is exactly the categorical imperative’s formula and morality’s principle. A free will and a will subject to moral laws are therefore one and the same.

If we presuppose freedom of the will, morality and its principle follow simply by analysing that concept. Yet the latter principle is synthetic: an absolutely good will is one whose maxim can always include itself as a universal law. Analysing the concept of an absolutely good will can never reveal this property of its maxim. Synthetic propositions are possible only when two cognitions are connected through a third in which both are found. The positive concept of freedom supplies this third cognition. Unlike physical causes, it cannot be the nature of the sensible world, whose concept joins something as cause to something else as effect. We cannot yet show what this third cognition is, towards which freedom points and of which we have an a priori idea. Nor can we yet explain how principles of pure practical reason establish the concept of freedom as legitimate, and with it the possibility of a categorical imperative. Further preparation is needed.
Freedom must be Presupposed as a Property of the Will
of every Rational Being

Whatever reasons we may have for attributing freedom to our own will, that is insufficient unless they also justify attributing it to every rational being. Morality is a law for us only because we are rational, so it must hold for every rational being. Since it must be deduced solely from freedom, we must show that freedom too belongs to all rational beings. Supposed experiences of human nature cannot suffice to prove it; indeed, such a proof is impossible, since freedom can be shown only a priori. We must establish that it belongs to the activity of all rational beings possessing a will. Now I maintain that any being able to act only under the idea of freedom is, for that very reason, genuinely free from a practical standpoint. Every law inseparably connected with freedom binds it exactly as though a theoretically conclusive proof had shown its will free in itself. * Furthermore, every rational being with a will must be credited with the idea of freedom and with acting entirely under that idea. In such a being we conceive practical reason, reason possessing causality in relation to its objects. But we cannot conceive reason as consciously allowing its judgements to be biased from elsewhere. The subject would then attribute its judgement not to its own reason but to an impulse. Reason must regard itself as the author of its principles, independent of external influences. As practical reason, or a rational being’s will, it must consequently regard itself as free. Such a being can have a will of its own only under the idea of freedom. We must therefore attribute this idea, practically, to every rational being.

* I assume freedom here merely as an idea rational beings presuppose in acting, thereby avoiding the need to prove it theoretically as well. The former, practical assumption alone is sufficient for my present purpose. Even without a successful speculative proof, a being that can act only with the idea of freedom is bound by the same laws as one that actually is free. We can thus avoid the burden imposed on theory.
The Interest Attached to the Ideas of Morality

We have finally traced the definite concept of morality back to freedom’s idea. We could not prove freedom actually belongs to us or to human nature. We saw only that it must be presupposed to conceive a being as rational, conscious of its causality regarding its actions—that is, as possessing a will. The very same grounds require us to attribute to every being with reason and will the capacity to determine itself to act under the idea of its freedom.

Presupposing these ideas also revealed a law: subjective principles of action, or maxims, must always be adopted so that they can also hold as objective, universal principles, serving as universal laws of our own making. But why must I submit to this principle simply as a rational being, thereby also subjecting every other rational being to it? I concede that no interest compels me, since that would not yield a categorical imperative. Yet I must take an interest in it and understand how this happens. Here an "I ought" is properly an "I would," valid for every rational being if reason determined its actions without obstruction. Beings like us, however, are also influenced by other springs, namely sensibility, and do not always do what reason alone would do. For us this necessity is expressed only as an "ought": subjective necessity differs from objective necessity.

It therefore seems that the moral law, the principle of autonomy of the will, is merely presupposed within freedom’s idea, and that we cannot independently prove its actuality or objective necessity. Even then, we would have gained something substantial by defining the true principle more precisely than before. But concerning its validity and the practical necessity of submitting to it, we would not have advanced at all. Why must the universal validity of our maxim as law limit our actions? What grounds the worth we assign to acting this way—a worth so great that no interest can surpass it? Why does a person believe he feels his personal worth through this alone, a worth beside which the value of agreeable or disagreeable circumstances counts as nothing? To all these questions, we could give no answer that would be satisfactory.

We do sometimes find ourselves interested in a personal quality without any interest in external circumstances, provided that quality makes us capable of sharing in such circumstances if reason were to distribute them. In other words, simply being worthy of happiness can interest us without the motive of enjoying that happiness. Yet this judgement merely results from the moral law’s importance, which we previously presupposed when the idea of freedom detached us from every empirical interest. We still cannot understand in this way why we ought to detach ourselves from those interests: why we should regard ourselves as free in action yet subject to certain laws, finding in our person alone a worth compensating for losing everything that makes our condition valuable. Nor do we understand how such action is possible—in other words, where the moral law’s binding force comes from.

We must frankly acknowledge an apparent circle from which escape seems impossible. We assume ourselves free among efficient causes so that we can conceive ourselves subject to moral laws among ends; then we regard ourselves as subject to those laws because we have attributed freedom of will to ourselves. Freedom and the will’s self-legislation are both autonomy and therefore reciprocal concepts. Precisely for that reason, neither can explain or ground the other. At most, for logical purposes, they can reduce apparently different concepts of the same object to a single concept, as different fractions of equal value are reduced to their lowest terms.

One further possibility still remains to us: to ask whether we occupy different standpoints when, through freedom, we think of ourselves as efficient causes a priori, and when we conceive ourselves through our actions as effects appearing before our eyes.

No subtle reflection is needed for an observation available even to the most ordinary understanding, though, in its own manner, it may grasp it through an obscure exercise of judgement that it calls feeling. Every "idea" arriving involuntarily, such as a sensory idea, reveals objects only in the way they affect us, leaving what they are in themselves entirely unknown to us. However closely and attentively understanding examines such "ideas," and whatever clarity it brings to them, they can yield knowledge only of appearances, never knowledge of things in themselves. Once we make this distinction—perhaps merely by noticing the difference between ideas received from outside, in which we are passive, and those we produce simply from ourselves, in which we display our own activity—we must acknowledge and presuppose something behind appearances that is not itself an appearance: things in themselves. Yet we must also admit that, because we can know them only as they affect us, we cannot approach them more closely or ever know what they are in themselves. This supplies a distinction, however crude, between a world of sense and a world of understanding. The former may vary with the differences between sensory impressions in different observers; the latter, underlying it, always remains the same. Even knowledge of oneself through internal sensation cannot reveal what one is in oneself. A person does not create himself, so to speak, and obtains his concept of himself empirically, not a priori. Naturally, then, even self-knowledge comes only through inner sense: through appearances of his nature and the way his consciousness is affected. Beyond these features of his subject, composed of mere appearances, he must necessarily posit something else as their basis: his ego, whatever its character in itself may be. In respect of mere perception and receptivity to sensations, he must therefore count himself as belonging to the world of sense. In respect of whatever pure activity he possesses—whatever reaches consciousness directly, rather than by affecting the senses—he must count himself as belonging to the intellectual world, of which he knows nothing further. Reflection must bring a person to this conclusion about everything that can be presented to him. Even people of the most ordinary understanding probably reach it: as we know, they readily suppose something invisible and independently active behind sensory objects. They spoil this insight, however, by immediately making that invisible something sensible again, wanting to turn it into an object of intuition. They become no wiser for it.

A human being really does find within himself a faculty distinguishing him from everything else, even from himself insofar as objects affect him: reason. As pure spontaneity, reason stands above even understanding. Understanding too is spontaneous, rather than merely containing, like sense, intuitions produced when things affect us and we are passive. Yet its activity can generate only concepts that bring sensory intuitions under rules and thereby unite them in a single consciousness. Without using sensibility, understanding could not think at all. In what I call ideas [ideal conceptions], reason instead displays such pure spontaneity that it goes far beyond everything sensibility can supply. Its most important function is to distinguish the world of sense from the world of understanding, thereby setting limits to understanding itself.

A rational being must therefore regard itself as intelligence, rather than in its lower faculties, as belonging to the world of understanding, not the world of sense. It thus has two standpoints for considering itself and recognising the laws governing its faculties’ exercise and consequently every action. As a member of the world of sense, it is subject to natural laws, heteronomy. As a member of the intelligible world, it is subject to laws independent of nature, grounded in reason alone rather than experience.

As a rational being, and consequently as a member of the intelligible world, a person can conceive his will’s causality only under the idea of freedom. Independence from the determining causes of the sensible world—an independence reason must always attribute to itself—is freedom. The idea of freedom is inseparable from autonomy, and autonomy from morality’s universal principle. Ideally, this principle grounds every rational being’s actions, just as natural law grounds all phenomena.

This removes our earlier suspicion of a hidden circle in arguing from freedom to autonomy and then to moral law. We feared we had put forward the idea of freedom merely for the moral law’s sake, only to turn around and derive that same law from freedom afterwards. We could then offer no genuine reason at all for the law, only present it as a petitio principii that well-disposed minds might gladly grant but that we could never put forward as a proposition capable of proof. We now see that conceiving ourselves as free places us within the world of understanding as its members. There we recognise autonomy of the will and its consequence, morality. Conceiving ourselves as under obligation, by contrast, regards us as belonging to the world of sense and simultaneously to the world of understanding.
How Is a Categorical Imperative Possible?

Every rational being considers itself, as intelligence, a member of the world of understanding. It calls its causality a will precisely as an efficient cause belonging to that world. Yet it is also conscious of belonging to the world of sense, where its actions appear as mere appearances [phenomena] of that causality. We cannot understand how these actions are possible through a causality unknown to us. Instead, as parts of the sensible world, they must be viewed as determined by other phenomena, desires and inclinations. If I belonged only to the world of understanding, all my actions would perfectly accord with autonomy of the pure will. If I belonged only to the world of sense, we would have to regard them as wholly conforming to the natural law of desires and inclinations, nature’s heteronomy. The first would rest on morality as supreme principle; the second on happiness. But the world of understanding grounds the world of sense and therefore its laws. It accordingly legislates directly for my will, which belongs entirely to the world of understanding, and must be conceived as doing so. Although from one side I must regard myself as a being in the world of sense, from the other I must recognise myself as intelligence subject to the law of the world of understanding: to reason, which contains this law in freedom’s idea, and therefore to autonomy of the will. I must consequently regard the world of understanding’s laws as imperatives for me, and actions conforming to them as duties.

Categorical imperatives are possible, then, because the idea of freedom makes me a member of an intelligible world. If I belonged to nothing else, every action of mine would always conform to autonomy of the will. But because I also intuit myself as belonging to the world of sense, my actions ought to conform. This categorical "ought" expresses a synthetic a priori proposition: to my will as affected by sensible desires we add the idea of that same will as belonging to the world of understanding, pure and practical in itself. The latter contains, according to reason, the supreme condition of the former. Similarly, we add concepts of understanding to sensory intuitions. Those concepts by themselves signify only regular form in general, yet this addition makes possible the synthetic a priori propositions on which all knowledge of physical nature rests.

Ordinary human reason’s practical use confirms this argument. Even the most accomplished villain, if accustomed to using reason at all, wishes he possessed the qualities displayed by examples of honest purpose, steadfast adherence to good maxims, sympathy, and general benevolence—even when they demand great sacrifices of advantage and comfort. His inclinations and impulses alone prevent him from achieving this within himself, and at the same time he wishes to escape those inclinations, burdensome even to him. This shows that in thought he places himself, with a will free from sensible impulses, in an order entirely different from his desires in the sensible sphere. He cannot expect that wish to gratify his desires or secure a condition satisfying any actual or possible inclination: that would destroy the superiority of the very idea eliciting the wish. He can expect only greater intrinsic worth in his own person. He imagines himself this better person when he adopts the standpoint of a member of the world of understanding. The idea of freedom, independence from determining causes in the world of sense, forces him involuntarily to that standpoint. There he recognises a good will that, by his own admission, legislates for the bad will he possesses as a member of the world of sense. Even in violating it, he acknowledges the law’s authority. What he morally "ought" to do is therefore what he necessarily "would" do as a member of the world of understanding. He conceives it as an "ought" only because he also regards himself as belonging to the world of sense.
The Ultimate Limits of All Practical Philosophy

Everyone attributes freedom of will to himself. Hence our judgements that certain actions ought to have been performed, although they were not. This freedom is not, and cannot be, a concept derived from experience. It persists even when experience shows the opposite of what, presupposing freedom, we conceive as its necessary consequences. Yet it is equally necessary that everything occurring be firmly determined by natural laws. This natural necessity is likewise not empirical, precisely because it contains the concept of necessity and therefore of a priori knowledge. Experience nevertheless confirms this concept of a natural system. Indeed, we must inevitably presuppose it if experience itself—a connected knowledge of sensory objects under general laws—is to be possible. Freedom is therefore only an idea of reason, its objective reality in itself uncertain. Nature, by contrast, is a concept of understanding whose reality is, and necessarily must be, demonstrated in examples of experience.

A dialectic of reason arises because freedom attributed to the will seems to contradict natural necessity. Confronted with these two paths, reason finds physical necessity the much better travelled and more suitable road for speculation. For practical purposes, however, freedom’s narrow footpath is the only route on which reason can guide our conduct. Neither the subtlest philosophy nor the most ordinary human reason can therefore argue freedom away. Philosophy must assume that freedom and physical necessity do not genuinely contradict one another in the same human actions. It can abandon the concept of nature no more than the concept of freedom.

Even if we never understand how freedom is possible, we must convincingly remove this apparent contradiction. If the thought of freedom contradicted itself or nature, which is equally necessary, it would have to be abandoned altogether in favour of physical necessity.

The contradiction would be inescapable if the thinking subject, which appears free to itself, conceived itself in exactly the same sense or relation when calling itself free and when regarding the same action as subject to natural law. It is therefore an indispensable task of speculative philosophy to show that this illusion of contradiction rests on our thinking of a person in different senses and different relations: when we call him free, and when we regard him as part of nature subject to its laws. It must show not only that these can coexist, but that they must be thought necessarily united in the same subject. Otherwise we could give no reason for burdening reason with an idea that may be reconciled without contradiction with another sufficiently established idea, yet entangles reason in a perplexity that gravely obstructs its theoretical use. This task belongs exclusively to speculative philosophy. The philosopher has no choice about resolving the apparent contradiction. If he leaves it untouched, the corresponding theory becomes bonum vacans, vacant property, which the fatalist could rightfully take over, expelling all morality from its supposed domain as an occupant without title.

We cannot yet say, however, that we have reached practical philosophy’s boundaries. Resolving this dispute is not its task. It merely demands that speculative reason end the discord into which theoretical questions lead it, so that practical reason can rest securely against external attacks that might render disputed the ground on which it intends to build.

Even ordinary reason’s claim to freedom of will rests on consciousness and the accepted presupposition that reason is independent of merely subjectively determining causes. Together, these causes constitute what belongs solely to sensation and so fall under the general heading sensibility. When a person considers himself as intelligence, he places himself in a different order and relates himself to entirely different determining grounds. On one side he thinks of himself as intelligence possessing a will and therefore causality; on the other he perceives himself as a phenomenon in the world of sense, which he really also is, and declares his causality externally determined according to natural laws. He soon sees that both accounts can, indeed must, hold simultaneously. There is not the slightest contradiction in a thing as appearance, belonging to the world of sense, being subject to laws from which that very thing or being in itself is independent. His need to think of himself in this double way rests, first, on consciousness of himself as an object affected through the senses; second, on consciousness of himself as intelligence, independent of sensory impressions in exercising reason—in other words, belonging to the world of understanding.

This explains why a person claims a will that disregards everything belonging to desires and inclinations. He conceives actions as possible, even necessary, for him that can be performed only by setting aside every desire and sensible inclination. Their causality lies in him as intelligence and in laws of effects and actions depending on principles of an intelligible world. He knows no more of that world than that pure reason alone, independently of sensibility, gives its laws. Moreover, only there, as intelligence, is he his proper self; as a human being he is merely the appearance of himself. Those laws therefore bind him directly and categorically. Inclinations and appetites—in other words, the whole nature of the world of sense—cannot undermine the laws of his willing as intelligence. He does not even hold himself responsible for those incitements or attribute them to his proper self, his will. He attributes to the will only the indulgence he might grant them by letting them influence his maxims at the expense of the will’s rational laws.

When practical reason thinks in this way, it does not exceed its own limits by thinking itself into a world of understanding, as it would by trying to enter through intuition or sensation. The former thought is merely negative towards the world of sense, which supplies no laws to reason in determining the will. It is positive in just one respect: freedom as a negative characteristic is also joined to a positive faculty, even a causality of reason, which we call a will. This is the faculty of acting so that actions’ principles conform to the essential character of a rational motive: that a maxim possess universal validity as law. If reason borrowed an object of willing, a motive, from the world of understanding, it would overstep its limits and claim knowledge of something it does not know. That world’s concept is only a standpoint reason must adopt outside appearances to conceive itself as practical. This would be impossible if sensible influences determined a person, but necessary unless we deny his consciousness of himself as intelligence and hence as a rational cause acting through reason, or freely. This thought certainly implies an order and system of laws different from the mechanism of nature in the sensible world. It makes necessary the concept of an intelligible world, the entire system of rational beings as things in themselves. Yet it does not entitle us to think further about that world than its formal condition: the universal validity of the will’s maxims as laws, and thus the will’s autonomy, which alone agrees with its freedom. Laws referring to a definite object, by contrast, produce heteronomy, belonging solely to natural laws and applying only to the sensible world.
Reason would, however, cross every boundary if it tried to explain how pure reason can be practical. That is exactly the same problem as explaining how freedom is possible.

We can explain only what can be brought under laws whose objects are given in some possible experience. Freedom is merely an idea whose objective reality cannot be shown through natural laws and thus cannot appear in any possible experience. Because no example or analogy can support it, we can never comprehend or understand it. It holds only as reason’s necessary hypothesis in a being that believes itself conscious of a will, a faculty distinct from mere desire: the faculty of determining itself to act as intelligence, through rational laws independently of natural instincts. Where determination by natural laws ends, explanation ends too. Only defence remains: removing the objections of those who claim deeper insight into things’ nature and boldly declare freedom impossible. We can only point out to them that the contradiction they suppose they have discovered arises in the following way. In order to apply the law of nature to human actions, they must necessarily consider a human being as an appearance. When we then ask them also to think of him as intelligence, as a thing in itself, they nevertheless persist in treating him as an appearance in this respect too. On those terms, it would indeed contradict itself to remove the same subject’s causality, his will, from every natural law of the sensible world. But the contradiction vanishes if they reflect and reasonably acknowledge that things in themselves, though hidden, must underlie appearances. We cannot expect their laws to be identical with the laws governing their appearances.

Our subjective inability to explain freedom of the will is identical with our inability to discover and explain the interest * a person can take in the moral law. Nevertheless, he actually does take such an interest. We call its basis within us moral feeling. Some have wrongly made this feeling the standard of moral judgement. It must instead be understood as the law’s subjective effect on the will, while reason alone supplies its objective principle.

* Interest is what makes reason practical, a cause determining the will. We therefore say only rational beings take an interest in something; non-rational beings merely feel sensual appetites. Reason takes a direct interest in action only when its maxims’ universal validity alone suffices to determine the will. Only this interest is pure. If reason can determine the will solely through another desired object or through a particular feeling in the subject, its interest in the action is indirect. Reason alone, without experience, cannot discover objects of the will or a particular feeling moving it. The latter interest is therefore merely empirical, not a pure rational interest. Reason’s logical interest, the extension of its insight, is never direct; it presupposes purposes for which reason is used.

For a rational being also affected by the senses to will what reason alone says it ought to will, reason must indeed be able to produce pleasure or satisfaction in fulfilling duty. It must possess a causality that determines sensibility according to its own principles. Yet we cannot understand a priori how a mere thought, containing nothing sensible, can itself produce a sensation of pleasure or pain. This is a particular kind of causality, and, as with any other causality, we can determine nothing about it a priori; we must consult experience alone. Experience, however, cannot supply us with any relation of cause and effect except a relation between two objects that are themselves both given in experience. Here, although the effect occurs within experience, the supposed cause is pure reason operating through mere ideas that supply experience with no object. It is therefore entirely beyond us to explain how or why the universal validity of a maxim as law—that is, morality—interests us. Only this is certain: its validity does not arise from our interest. That would be heteronomy, practical reason depending on sensibility, a feeling as its principle, and therefore unable to give moral laws. Instead, it interests us because it holds for us as human beings, originating in our will as intelligences, our proper self. Reason necessarily subordinates what belongs to mere appearance to the nature of the thing in itself.

We can therefore answer "How a categorical imperative is possible," only this far: we can identify its sole enabling hypothesis, the idea of freedom, and recognise that this hypothesis is necessary. This suffices for reason’s practical exercise, for conviction of the imperative’s validity and hence of the moral law. But how this hypothesis itself can be possible is something that no human reason can ever discover or make intelligible to itself. If an intelligence’s will is free, autonomy necessarily follows as the essential formal condition determining it. Moreover, as speculative philosophy can show, this freedom of will is possible as a hypothesis: it does not contradict physical necessity in the connections among sensible phenomena. Beyond that, a rational being conscious of causality through reason—of a will distinct from desires—must necessarily make freedom, practically and in idea, the condition of every voluntary action. What exceeds human reason is explaining how pure reason can be practical by itself without a spring of action from another source. How can the mere principle of all its maxims’ universal validity as laws—the very form of pure practical reason—provide a spring of action without any matter or object of the will in which we could first take an interest? How can it produce an interest called purely moral? To explain this, or how pure reason can be practical, exceeds human reason’s power. All effort spent seeking that explanation is wasted.

It is exactly as though I sought to discover how freedom itself is possible as a will’s causality. I would leave the ground of philosophical explanation without having any other ground to stand on. I might revel in the remaining world of intelligences, but a well-founded idea of it gives me not the slightest knowledge of it. No effort of my natural rational faculty could ever yield such knowledge. It signifies only what remains after I eliminate everything sensible from the principles moving my will. It serves merely to keep motives drawn from sensibility within bounds, marking their limits and showing that they do not contain everything: there is something beyond them, though I know nothing further about it. Once all matter, all knowledge of objects, is abstracted from the pure reason forming this ideal, only form remains: the practical law of maxims’ universality. Corresponding to this is the conception of reason, in relation to a pure world of understanding, as a possible efficient cause determining the will. Springs of action must be entirely absent here, unless the very idea of an intelligible world is itself the spring, or that in which reason first takes an interest. But making that intelligible is precisely the problem we cannot solve.

This is the ultimate boundary of all moral inquiry. Identifying it is important even simply to prevent reason from making two errors. On one side, it must not harm morality by searching the world of sense for a supreme motive and an intelligible but empirical interest. On the other, it must not flap its wings helplessly in the space of transcendent concepts we call the intelligible world, a space empty for reason, losing itself among fantasies without advancing. Nevertheless, the idea of a pure world of understanding remains useful and legitimate for rational belief: a system of all intelligences to which we belong as rational beings, although we also belong to the sensible world. All knowledge stops at its threshold. Its use is to awaken a lively interest in the moral law through the noble ideal of a universal kingdom of ends in themselves, rational beings. We can belong as members only by carefully conducting ourselves according to maxims of freedom as though they were laws of nature.
Concluding Remark

Reason’s speculative use concerning nature leads to the absolute necessity of a supreme cause of the world. Its practical use concerning freedom also leads to absolute necessity, but only of the laws governing a rational being’s actions as such. Whatever its use, reason essentially seeks to advance its knowledge to consciousness of necessity; without that, the knowledge would not be rational. Yet reason is equally restricted: it cannot understand the necessity of what exists, what happens, or what ought to happen unless it presupposes a condition under which it exists, happens, or ought to happen. Continually asking for the condition, however, only postpones reason’s satisfaction further and further. Reason therefore endlessly seeks the unconditionally necessary and feels compelled to assume it, without being able to make it comprehensible. It is fortunate even to find a concept consistent with that assumption. Our inability to conceive the absolute necessity of an unconditional practical law, as the categorical imperative must be, is therefore no defect in our deduction of morality’s supreme principle. It is an objection to human reason generally. Reason cannot be blamed for refusing to explain this necessity through a condition, an interest assumed as a foundation: that would deprive the law of its status as reason’s supreme law. We do not comprehend the moral imperative’s unconditional practical necessity, but we do comprehend its incomprehensibility. That is all we can fairly demand of a philosophy striving to carry its principles to the very boundary of human reason.
